Gowon’s memoirs: Nigeria owes Awolowo an eternal debt, by Olu Fasan
items.description: Last week, I started a discussion of General Yakubu Gowon’s multi-themed memoirs, My Life of Duty & Allegiance. My focus was on the book’s general tone, which I find unduly self-justificatory. In his attempts to defend his legacy, General Gowon presents himself as a saintly figure who did no wrong as a leader, whereas some introspection and nuanced reflection would have helped. That said, the book is a treasure trove of insightful details that enrich our historical narrative. This week, I will focus on one of such insights, namely, the quality of governance and public service ethos under General Gowon’s regime, with Chief Obafemi Awolowo singled out as the arrowhead of a remarkable governance approach that, if replicated today, would transform how Nigeria is governed and, thus, this country’s fortunes. As a political economist and policy practitioner who spent nearly 20 years advising the UK government on diverse policy areas, in addition to teaching public policy, I have professional and intellectual interests in how government is run. Thus, I was enthralled by General Gowon’s fascinating accounts of how the affairs of state were conducted under his administration, with the triumvirate of politicians (as ministers), civil servants (as technocrats), and universities and think-tanks (as sounding boards) driving policy formulation and implementation and setting standards of good and effective governance. Sitting atop the triumvirate was Chief Awolowo, an extraordinarily transformative leader! Indeed, if General Gowon’s memoirs can be said to have a hero, that hero is Chief Obafemi Awolowo, appointed by Gowon as the Vice Chairman of the Federal Executive Council, FEC, and Commissioner of Finance in his administration. In every reference to Chief Awolowo in the memoirs, General Gowon writes glowingly and superlatively about him. Gowon also gives credit to his colleagues in the Supreme Military Council, SMC, and the first-class mandarins who ran the civil service for his administration’s successes, especially its ability to prosecute a 30-month civil war “without endangering the national economy”. But he reserves his most generous praise for Chief Awolowo. Hear Gowon: “Chief Awolowo’s business acumen, political sagacity, economic wizardry and thorough man-management ability would later prove quite useful and helpful in ensuring that we kept our finances intact during and immediately after the civil war that broke out a few weeks after his appointment to the FEC.” He adds: “Without any argument, he made invaluable contributions.” Of course, Chief Awolowo’s reputation preceded him. As the premier of the Western Region, he performed so superbly that Harold Wilson, then British prime minister, described him as a “world-class leader”, who would make an outstanding President of America or Prime Minister of Britain. General Gowon himself referenced Chief Awolowo’s pedigree, saying that he appointed him as the Commissioner of Finance with concurrent responsibility as Vice-Chairman of the FEC “because of his experience in politics and management of the economy of the old Western Region.” Indeed, General Gowon was so enamoured of Chief Awolowo that he admits in his memoirs that one of his administration’s flagship policies, the Universal Primary Education, UPE, was based on a policy introduced by Chief Awolowo as premier. “In scope and content,” Gowon writes, “UPE was not radically different from the model that was initiated by Chief Awolowo in the defunct Western Region while he was the Premier.” Two lessons emerge from this narrative. First, good leaders get the brightest and best in their teams; they form what a British prime minister described as GOATs (“Government of All the Talents”). Second, good leaders embrace good ideas and best practices worldwide. Indeed, one of the universally recognised approaches to sound policymaking is international comparison, which allows a government to consider what works elsewhere. Sadly, neither lesson is embedded in governance in Nigeria today. For instance, today, a Nigerian leader would fill his cabinet with cronies and political jobbers rather than seasoned technocrats and brilliant administrators. There’s also the phenomenon of policy discontinuities. Virtually every government won’t complete projects started by its predecessor, let alone copy sensible policies elsewhere, resulting in widespread abandoned projects and policy failures. But there’s another unlearned lesson. Chief Awolowo was never a yes-man in General Gowon’s government. Gowon himself cites two instances to prove this. In both instances, General Gowon eventually had his way, but Awolowo laid down the marker. In one case, General Gowon procured the services of a Lebanese contractor for the government. But Chief Awolowo refused to approve payment to the contractor, arguing that “the process of getting help from the Lebanese was not properly followed and documented and, as such, was an extra-budgetary expenditure.” Tell me, how many extra-budgetary expenditures are waived through without due process today? Can a finance minister challenge a president’s frivolous spending today? In another case, Chief Awolowo refused to approve a request for additional money for Gowon’s upkeep after the original budget was exhausted. He argued that the possibility of overshoots should have been considered before the budget was prepared and approved. This is how Gowon puts it in his memoirs: “Everyone knew how difficult it was to get anything out of Chief Awolowo without well-reasoned arguments.” What an extraordinary testimonial! But where are such principled and painstakingly meticulous ministers and public officers in Nigeria today? Sadly, none! To be sure, a tree does not make a forest, and Chief Awolowo did not act alone. As premier of the Western Region and later as Commissioner for Finance and Vice Chairman of the FEC, Chief Awolowo was surrounded by outstanding colleagues and civil servants. For instance, General Gowon mentions the sterling role of Professor Adebayo Adedeji, the world-renowned economist, who was the Commissioner for Economic Development. And talking about bureaucrats, who can forget the “Super Perm Secs” of the Gowon era? As the German sociologist and political economist Max Weber put it, “the state will not conduct its affairs without the bureaucracy.” Oxbridge-educated mandarins like Ahmed Joda, Allison Ayida and Philip Asiodu led what Gowon describes as “the deeply cerebral, committed and efficient technocrats in the civil service”, which he calls “the engine room” of his government. But where are today’s “super perm secs”? Where is today’s vibrant and technocratic civil service? Sadly, today, Nigeria has one of the worst civil services in the world, a subject I discuss in my book, In The National Interest, arguing that the collapse of the civil service and the public sector in general is at the heart of Nigeria’s acutely weak state capacity. As a scholar-practitioner, I was also excited about General Gowon’s accounts of how his government worked closely with universities. He writes: “We made exceptionally effective use of the many eggheads that populated the various university campuses to shape the policy directions.” He adds: “Many of the dons at the university were our formal and informal sounding boards for policy formulations and analyses.” In the UK, the government works in tandem with universities and think-tanks to shape policies. Sadly, in Nigeria, the government is anti-intellectual, with academics and think-tanks ostracised and treated as pariahs, rarely engaged in policy development. General Gowon makes another profound point about the policy process, saying: “These policies were not unilateral decisions. We diligently thought through the policies, and we implemented them based on their overall benefits to the people.” Compare that with how President Tinubu impulsively removed the fuel subsidy after he was “possessed by courage”, with zero consideration of the impacts on the people! Truth be told, General Gowon led an extremely effective government, with the prudent management of the economy during the civil war, without external borrowing, a genuine candidate for the Guinness Book of Records. Indeed, Nigeria managed its finances so well that the World Bank borrowed money from the country. Yet crude oil was selling for just $15 per barrel, while Nigeria was pumping just about 1.2m barrels per day. Today, in peacetime, with crude selling for nearly $100 per barrel and Nigeria pumping nearly 2mn barrels per day, the government is borrowing excessively. General Gowon hails Chief Awolowo’s “economic wizardry”. He’s right. But Awolowo didn’t just save Nigeria from economic collapse during and after the war; he also set world-class standards on how to run a country. Nigeria is eternally in his debt! The post Gowon’s memoirs: Nigeria owes Awolowo an eternal debt, by Olu Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The US built world’s greatest card system
items.description: By YVONNE-FAITH ELAIGWU The history of payments is, in many ways, the history of making value easier to move. We started at barter and are now at electronic transfers, with stablecoins suggesting that the next evolution is here. New payment methods rarely make their predecessors useless. Cash did not immediately eliminate barter. Cards did not eliminate cheques. Account-to-account payments will not eliminate cards. But payments evolve. And one of the most interesting examples of that evolution can be found in an unlikely comparison: Nigeria and the United States. The United States built perhaps the world’s greatest card ecosystem. Nigeria just seems to have built past it. The American card system is extraordinary. Over decades, the U.S. built an ecosystem connecting consumers, merchants, issuing banks, acquiring banks, and card networks. Around it grew credit bureaus, credit scores, revolving credit, chargebacks, fraud protection, loyalty points, airline miles, and billions of dollars of rewards. Consequently, Americans have a compelling reason to use cards. And use them, they do. Data from the Federal Reserve show that credit-card payments reached 67.1 billion transactions in 2024, while ACH processed an enormous $104.06 trillion in 2024. America, therefore, doesn’t lack account-to-account infrastructure. The difference is where A2A sits in everyday consumer behaviour. Walk into an American store, and the natural question is still: Which card am I using? In Nigeria, increasingly, a different question is asked: “What is your account number?” That difference is more significant than it appears. Nigeria took another road. Nigeria never developed America’s deep credit-card culture. Debit cards became widespread, but cards did not become as deeply embedded in the country’s economic architecture as they did in America. Instead, Nigeria increasingly solved digital payments at the bank-account level. At the centre of this transformation is the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System and its NIBSS Instant Payment platform, built to operate 24/7 with most transactions settling in under one second. This infrastructure changed behaviour. Any individual or company can pay another individual or merchant, and the transaction can be executed on a Friday evening or a Sunday morning. The expectation is still remarkably simple: the money should arrive now. That expectation is one of Nigeria’s greatest payment achievements. America’s success may be part of its problem. This is where the comparison becomes fascinating. America isn’t stuck on cards because it cannot build something better. It may be stuck on cards partly because cards work so well. The merchant already has the terminal. The consumer already has the card. The bank earns card revenue. Visa and Mastercard provide enormous networks. Consumers receive points, miles, fraud protection, and access to credit. Everyone has something to lose from changing the system. Even the Federal Reserve has acknowledged the economic tension. The better yesterday’s infrastructure becomes, the harder tomorrow’s infrastructure can be to adopt. Nigeria had a different incentive. Nigeria faced different circumstances. Card payments existed, but the country had stronger incentives to develop alternative digital rails. Rather than building everything around the card, Nigeria created interoperable infrastructure allowing value to move directly between accounts. The result is not perfect. Instant payments introduce their own fraud problems. So, this is not an argument that cards are bad. Cheques aren’t bad either. They are simply technologies belonging to particular stages in the evolution of payments. America is catching up. The United States has recognized the need for real-time payments. The Clearing House launched RTP in 2017, and in July 2023, the Federal Reserve launched FedNow, allowing participating financial institutions to transfer funds in near real time, 24/7/365. The rails now exist. The challenge is making instant A2A payments as culturally normal at the American checkout as tapping a credit card. Nigeria has already crossed much of that behavioural bridge. It has also established formal Open Banking guidelines. There is a broader lesson here: technological development isn’t always linear. Sometimes, developing countries do not follow developed countries through every generation of infrastructure. They skip one. America perfected the card. Nigeria had less reason to protect it. And that may have made it easier to build what comes after it. *Elaigwu is an experienced operations leader with a background in financial services and corporate social responsibility. She is currently Head of Operations at OnePipe, where she drives customer experience and governance. The post The US built world’s greatest card system appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027 Elections: Beyond INEC, 375 Judges’ integrity under trial
items.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri With the 2027 general elections just 65 days away, all eyes are on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to conduct a smooth, free, fair, and credible poll. Meanwhile, preparations for the aftermath are already under way. A total of 375 judges have been nominated to serve on election petition tribunals, where they will adjudicate disputes brought by candidates and parties dissatisfied with the results. The judges, drawn from courts across the federation, were inaugurated on Monday, November 9, at a ceremony held at the Body of Benchers Complex in Abuja. Section 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, vests in the President of the Court of Appeal the responsibility for constituting election petition tribunals to adjudicate disputes arising from National and State Houses of Assembly and governorship elections. Similarly, section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, prescribes the timelines for constituting the tribunals and opening their registries. The swearing-in, organised by the President of the Court of Appeal, Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem, marked the formal assumption of a responsibility with considerable constitutional, professional and public significance. A three-day intensive workshop followed immediately. It was designed to deepen the judges’ knowledge of the Electoral Act 2026, familiarise them with applicable practice directions and the evolving jurisprudence of the courts on election-related cases, and sharpen the practical skills needed for case management, evaluation of evidence, control of proceedings, and the delivery of clear, well-reasoned judgments within the prescribed timelines. The CJN also used the occasion to launch the second edition of the Judicial Electoral Manual (JEM), which she said will help judicial officers locate relevant authorities, appreciate the development of the law and approach recurring issues with greater clarity. According to the CJN, by bringing together the relevant constitutional provisions, the Electoral Act 2026, applicable practice directions and judicial decisions, the Manual provides a useful resource for judicial officers and other stakeholders in the electoral adjudicatory process. She was quick to warn, however, that it should serve only as a guide and a reference tool. It does not replace independent judicial reasoning or relieve any judicial officer of the duty to consider each case on its own facts, the arguments of counsel and the applicable law. The Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, said the early swearing-in of the tribunal judges was a clear demonstration of the judiciary’s commitment to ensuring that electoral disputes are handled promptly, competently and in accordance with the law. Fagbemi noted that election petition tribunals occupy a unique position in Nigeria’s democratic architecture, which is why the adjudication of electoral disputes continues to attract intense public attention and scrutiny. By providing the constitutional mechanism through which electoral grievances are peacefully resolved, he said, the tribunals are indispensable to political stability and public trust in the electoral process. The AGF drew attention to the far-reaching reforms introduced by the Electoral Act 2026, which he said aim to strengthen electoral transparency, promote internal party democracy, modernise electoral administration and redefine the framework for electoral disputes. The Act restricts judicial intervention in internal party affairs. Section 83(5) ousts the jurisdiction of the courts over disputes concerning the internal affairs of political parties, while Section 83(6) stipulates sanctions for intra-party litigation. The Act restricts interim and interlocutory injunctions in prohibited intra-party proceedings, provides for accelerated hearings, and prescribes minimum costs of N10 million each against the litigant and counsel. Likewise, Section 138(1) limits the grounds for election petitions. The amended law confines election petitions to corrupt practices, substantial non-compliance with electoral law, and failure to secure a majority of lawful votes. Significantly, it omits candidate disqualification as an express post-election ground, potentially shifting qualification disputes to pre-election proceedings. The AGF argued that the innovations in the amended Act represent a significant recalibration of Nigeria’s electoral framework ahead of the general elections. “Their ultimate transformative impact will depend on effective enforcement by INEC, compliance by political parties and judicial interpretation,” he added. For the INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, SAN, electoral litigation has become increasingly complex. He observed that, beyond the familiar questions of voting, counting and collation, disputes now concern voter accreditation, electronic transmission of results, technological failures, the integrity of digital records, party primaries, candidate nominations and the conduct of election officials. He said the Electoral Act 2026 has provided the legislative framework for the forthcoming general elections. “Of particular relevance is Section 60(3), which addresses electronic transmission of polling-unit results and the legal implications of communication failures. “Its interpretation, alongside other provisions of the new Act, may feature prominently in future petitions. “The deployment of the BVAS and the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV) has brought greater technological sophistication to election administration and public access to electoral information. “At the same time, these systems raise questions about the authenticity, admissibility and probative value of electronic records, their relationship with physical documents, and the consequences of technical disruptions. “A clear distinction must be maintained between the generation of technological information, the statutory purpose it serves and the legal standard required to prove a case before a tribunal. “The distinction between pre-election matters and post-election petitions must be carefully observed,” the INEC Chairman added. Although INEC and the judiciary perform distinct but complementary constitutional functions, the credibility of the elections cannot be judged solely by the conduct of voting or the declaration of results. It will also depend on public confidence that electoral disputes will be determined independently, fairly and in accordance with the law. As the CJN pointed out, the 2027 elections will be a defining moment in the nation’s democratic journey. She warned that the courtroom must not become an extension of the political arena, stressing that disputes must be resolved on the basis of the pleadings, evidence and applicable law. Of the 375 judges nominated, 138 have previous tribunal experience, while 237 are new to such proceedings. The workshop is expected to have equipped them with the skills and knowledge to navigate the murky waters of election litigation and arrive at legally sound decisions. By fairly determining any disputes arising from the 2027 elections, the judiciary stands to safeguard the people’s mandate, uphold constitutional supremacy and sustain public confidence in democratic governance. The post 2027 Elections: Beyond INEC, 375 Judges’ integrity under trial appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Thinking on your feet: The power of spoken structure under pressure, by Ruth Oji
items.description: Among the many communication challenges professionals encounter, few produce as much immediate anxiety as being asked an unexpected question in a public setting. The scenario is familiar to almost everyone: You are sitting in a department review, an academic seminar, an industry panel, or a client briefing. Without warning, the chairperson turns to you and says, “What are your thoughts on this proposal?” or “How should we handle this unexpected operational delay?” In that single second, your heart rate increases, adrenaline surges, and your mind races. You have relevant experience and informed opinions, but under the sudden spotlight of the room, your working memory feels temporarily paralyzed. Fearing that silence will make you look unprepared, you begin speaking immediately. You offer a few polite disclaimers, describe unrelated background context, and circle around three different ideas, hoping that a coherent conclusion will emerge along the way. By the time you finish two minutes later, you are out of breath, the room is slightly confused, and you realize you never directly answered the question. This common struggle is not a measure of intelligence, dedication, or professional competence. It is simply a structural problem. When put on the spot, you cannot rely on unstructured improvisation; you need a clear, dependable mental framework to organize your thoughts under pressure. The Cognitive Dilemma of Spontaneous Speech To understand why spontaneous speaking feels difficult, it helps to examine what happens to our thinking process under sudden stress. When you are asked an unexpected question in front of your peers or superiors, your brain experiences a mild threat response. Adrenaline floods your system, narrowing your focus and reducing your working memory capacity. In this heightened state, attempting to simultaneously decide what you want to say, how you want to sequence your arguments, and when you are going to stop speaking creates heavy cognitive overload. Without a roadmap, speakers instinctively resort to “verbal stall tactics”—rambling introductions, excessive throat-clearing, and endless qualifications—while their brains frantically search for a central point. The solution to this dilemma is not to try harder or speak faster. The solution is to separate the structure of your answer from the content. When you have a simple, pre-learned structural template stored in your memory, you no longer need to invent an organizational method in real time. The template holds the shape of your ideas, freeing your mind to focus entirely on sharing your perspective clearly and calmly. The Architecture of the PREP Method One of the most effective and versatile mental models for impromptu speaking is the PREP Framework. Originally developed in classical rhetoric and refined in modern executive training, PREP stands for four clear, sequential stages: Point, Reason, Example, Point. [ Point ] – State your core recommendation or conclusion directly. [ Reason ] – Explain the primary logic or data supporting your point. [ Example ] – Provide a concrete illustration, past metric, or case study. [ Point ] – Restate your core recommendation with a clear call to action. Let us examine each stage in practical terms: Point: Lead with the Conclusion The most critical habit in spontaneous communication is stating your main takeaway in the very first sentence. In formal writing, we often build up to our conclusion through pages of analysis. In spoken conversation, however, listeners need to know your destination immediately. When you open with a clear, direct statement—such as “I recommend we pause the maintenance schedule on Line 2 until Monday”—you give your listeners a mental hook. They now know exactly what you are proposing, making it easy for them to follow the supporting details that follow. Leading with your point also eliminates the nervous habit of opening with apologetic padding, such as “Well, I haven’t looked at all the latest reports yet, but maybe…” Directness is not arrogance; it is a courteous way to value the room’s time. Reason: Provide the Core Logical Driver Once your point is on the table, immediately explain the primary reason behind it. The reason answers the listener’s immediate question: “Why do you say that?” Keep your reason focused on a single, compelling argument rather than listing five secondary factors. For instance: “Because the weather forecast indicates high winds that exceed our safety operating limits for crane deployment.” By offering one clear, substantive reason, you provide solid logical backing without overwhelming your listeners with unnecessary detail. Example: Anchor Your Logic in Concrete Reality Abstract arguments are easy to forget; concrete examples are easy to understand and remember. In the third stage of PREP, provide a brief piece of evidence, a specific past experience, or a concrete data point that proves your reason. For example: “Last October, when a team operated under similar wind conditions at the offshore terminal, equipment was damaged and operations were delayed by forty-eight hours.” Grounding your argument in a factual example moves the discussion from subjective opinion to objective reality. It gives your listeners a tangible reference point that reinforces your credibility. Point: Close the Loop Cleanly The final step is restating your original point in a decisive concluding sentence. Many professionals give an excellent explanation and share a great example, only to finish with an awkward fade: “…and, yeah, so, that’s basically what I was thinking.” A weak ending dilutes the impact of everything that came before. Instead, close the loop by restating your core recommendation: “Therefore, postponing the maintenance to Monday protects our personnel and ensures the work is completed safely.” Restating your point signals clearly that you have finished speaking, leaving the room with a crisp, professional conclusion. Applying the Model Across Industries The strength of the PREP model lies in its universal adaptability. It functions equally well across varied professional and academic contexts: In Technology: Point: “We should implement automated testing for this billing module.” Reason: “Because manual testing is taking two full engineering days per release cycle.” Example: “During our last release, three minor edge-case errors slipped through and caused billing ticket spikes.” Point: “Automating this test suite will shorten our release cycle and maintain software quality.” In Energy and Operations: Point: “We need to upgrade the pressure monitoring sensors at Station B.” Reason: “The current analog sensors are reaching their end-of-life reliability limits.” Example: “Over the past month, our field technicians had to perform three manual recalibrations during operating hours.” Point: “Replacing these units during the scheduled shutdown will prevent unexpected downtime.” In Higher Education and Research: Point: “The study’s conclusion regarding student engagement needs qualification.” Reason: “The underlying research methodology relies exclusively on self-reported surveys rather than behavioral metrics.” Example: “In Section 3, over forty percent of participants acknowledged they completed the questionnaire in a single sitting without verifying their study hours.” Point: “To make broader claims about academic habits, we need longitudinal tracking data.” Structure as the Foundation of Confidence There is a common misconception that having a structured approach restricts your personality, making you sound rigid or scripted. In practice, the opposite is true. When you do not have a reliable framework, nervous energy consumes your attention. You become preoccupied with managing your own uncertainty. But when you trust a reliable mental structure like PREP, the scaffolding handles the organization for you. Your cognitive energy is freed to focus on warmth, eye contact, and genuine connection with your colleagues. Confidence in communication is rarely a magical personality trait reserved for natural extroverts. It is the natural result of having dependable tools that function under pressure. The next time an unexpected question is directed your way in a meeting, resist the urge to rush into speech or fill the silence with rambling disclaimers. Take a calm breath, identify your core point, support it with a clear reason and example, and close the loop decisively. By making structured thinking a daily habit, you will find that thinking on your feet becomes one of your greatest professional strengths. The post Thinking on your feet: The power of spoken structure under pressure, by Ruth Oji appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: What, if the heavens fall? By Ikechukwu Amaechi
items.description: Following the November 5, ruling of Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, which nullified the Senator David Mark leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and invalidated all decisions taken under his watch, including the primary elections that produced the party’s candidates for the 2027 elections, Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, is behaving like the overfed little bird Nza in Igbo folklore that challenged his Chi (personal god) to a bout. Many Nigerians were aghast at the judge’s indiscretion and absolute lack of emotional intelligence when he voided not only the candidacy of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar but also every other ticket of the party simply because of the contrived grievance of one Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former official of the party. But Keyamo is over the moon with the consequential judgement, which import according to one of Gombe’s counsel, Luka Musa Haruna, a learned silk, is that, “As it stands today, the ADC has no candidate from the presidential level to the House of Assembly, governorship, Senate and all other elective positions for the 2027 election,” because apparently he sees in the defanging of the ADC even before the first ballot is cast the only pathway to the All Progressives Congress (APC) victory. It didn’t bother Keyamo, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN) that the judgement was delivered only 72 days to the polls, a brazen and rascally act of judicial mischief by a judge whose actions were recently described by a three-member panel of the Court of Appeal led by Justice A. B. Mohammed as rendering him “unfit for the bench.” To every discerning observer of the unfolding political drama, the fact that the judgement ousting ADC, the main opposition party, from the 2027 ballot, was delivered barely 24 hours after Atiku, commenced his nation-wide campaigns with a hugely successful rally in Sokoto State, is telling both in reality and optics. It was a panic move by a ruling party afraid of competition. But Keyamo would rather gaslight Nigerians with his jejune “Heavens will not fall if a certain Atiku Abubakar is not on the ballot in 2027” rhetoric. Sheer orotundity borne out of fear. As a lawyer, Keyamo knows that the dictum “heavens will not fall,” derived from the Latin legal maxim Fiat justitia ruat caelum – Let justice be done, though the heavens fall – in principle attests to the inviolability of justice when the law is applied fairly, no matter the cost. In other words, it speaks to a strict moral and legal commitment to judicial integrity. So, heavens are not expected to fall when the courts and those in power do not bend the rules. But heavens definitely will fall in a situation where a judge recently lampooned by brother-judges on a superior bench as someone whose actions constitute the “gravest form of judicial misconduct” and “highest form of judicial impertinence” whimsically gives a ruling that flushes the candidacy of Atiku and his running mate, Rotimi Amaechi, 28 governorship hopefuls and their running mates, 346 House of Representatives and 108 senatorial candidates and thousands of House of Assembly contestants down APC’s invidious toilet of political mischief. Granted, because this is Nigeria, Lifu’s ruling could be upheld even by superior courts with the hope that nothing will happen. After all, what have we not seen? But if that is what gives Keyamo and his ilk the audacity to ride roughshod over fellow citizens, they are definitely not reading the tea leaves. Because if they are, they would have noticed that opposition political parties are no longer running away from state-sponsored thugs. They are increasingly confronting them. When the Sokoto State government denied the ADC venues for their campaigns, they took the rally to the streets and the entire state was shut down. Heavens fall when citizens have it up to their necks and insensitive leaders taunt them for their predicament as Senator Abdul’aziz Yari, Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, did this week in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, when he told poor Nigerians: “You are hungry because you are lazy. If you work hard, you will not be hungry.” Heavens fall when the inordinate ambition of men of power blights their sense of reasoning. Heavens fall when leaders become too arrogant to care about the consequences of their actions. Despite our legendary reputation for docility, the ramparts of ‘heaven’ as constructed by foolhardy and vainglorious politicians begin to crack when the people are pushed to the wall and urged to take a swim in a shark-infested lagoon if they grumble. And that is exactly what the APC is doing right now. That is why Keyamo’s “heavens will not fall” rhetoric is extremely dangerous. Anyone who supports the exclusion of Atiku and the entire ADC cast of candidates from the 2027 ballot at this late hour does not mean well for the country. This is neither about Atiku Abubakar nor ADC. It is about Nigeria and the inalienable right of citizens to choose their leaders without let or hindrance. It is about the peculiar circumstances of our fragile statehood. It was for this same reason that the General Abdulsalami Abubakar-led junta registered the Alliance for Democracy (AD) in 1998 even when it didn’t meet the registration criteria. In his autobiography, Call of Duty, the former Head of State wrote: “We had to apply some wisdom and flexibility. As projected, the AD eventually didn’t meet the criteria for the registration of political parties. We tinkered with the rules and said any party that came third would be registered. That was how AD scaled through. We did not want to create a system in which the South-West would feel marginalised. Whatever decision we took was for the peace and progress of the country. If tinkering with the rule we made ourselves would give respite to Nigerians, why not? The rules were made by humans and for humans. The idea was to give peace a chance and to ensure that there was equity and justice.” It is imprudent for anyone to think that there will be no consequences for government’s bad behaviour, no matter how egregious because Nigeria is a captured state where citizens have been abused to submission. History does not validate such hypothesis. If only our leaders learn from history, they would know that no matter the vicious inclination of a country’s security forces, they are never a match to a people with their back against the wall. Last year, President Andry Rajoelina of Madagascar fled his Indian Ocean island nation following weeks of youth-led and Gen Z anti-government protests over severe power and water shortages, corruption, and economic hardships. In August 2024, Bangladesh’s longest-serving Prime Minister, Sheikh Hasina, was forced to resign and flee the country after waves of protests toppled her government. In July 2022, President Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled Sri Lanka after months of mass protests triggered by a crippling economic collapse, severe food and fuel shortages, and anger against the ruling family. These are leaders who once believed like the current Nigerian leaders that they were invincible and the heavens will never fall because they had become the state writ large. In fact, in the case of Prime Minister Hasina, an estimated 1,400 people were killed by security forces who cracked down on the student-led protests that lasted for weeks. But she ultimately fled when she realised that rather than dampening their enthusiasm and weakening their resolve, the blood of their fallen compatriots emboldened the protesters and aggravated the protests. Those who relish lying to themselves could indulge their fantasy, but the truth staring us in the face is that Nigerian politicians are not planning for free, fair and credible elections in January. Weaponising the judiciary against the opposition as the APC is doing is an ill-wind. Using state governors to deny opposition parties level playing field is a recipe for chaos. Unleashing thugs on opposition leaders is a recipe for crisis. Using the judiciary to deny the opposition a foothold in the 2027 elections as Justice Lifu did with his ADC ruling is reckless. And boasting like Keyamo did that these shenanigans can endure without the heavens falling is crass ignorance and the height of foolhardiness. Time to pull back from the brink is now because the heavens can, indeed, fall when reason takes a flight. The post What, if the heavens fall? By Ikechukwu Amaechi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Gbenga Omotoso at 65: A rare gift of generosity and mentorship
items.description: By ROBERT UWEMEDIMO When Debbi Fields observed that “there is no such thing as coincidence; people come into our lives for a reason,” she captured a truth I have come to know profoundly through my relationship with Mr. Gbenga Omotoso. As he turned 65 on November 11, 2026, I pause to reflect on the extraordinary journey of more than two decades I have been privileged to share with the man I call boss – one who has been to me a father, mentor, benefactor, teacher, and, above all, a blessing from God Almighty. April 21, 2004, marked the beginning of a journey that would forever alter the course of my life. As I approached the wine-coloured plywood door on the second floor of a six-storey building at Ijora Causeway, Lagos – then the headquarters of The Comet newspaper – I opened it and found myself face to face with Mr. Omotoso, the Daily Editor, who needed someone to run errands for his office. He asked my name. “Robert,” I replied. “When will you resume work?” he asked. I was stunned. Here stood a man offering me a job before I had even applied; no interview, no credentials to present, no long queue outside a human resources office. Just one simple question that would rewrite the course of my life. “Tomorrow, sir,” I answered. That brief exchange marked the beginning of a relationship that shaped my life in ways I could never have imagined. I was a young boy who had lost his father at twelve. Little did I know that God was preparing another father figure for me in the person of Mr. Omotoso. When The Comet closed in 2006, a deep and overwhelming sense of uncertainty settled over us. Yet Mr. Omotoso looked me in the eye and assured me that wherever his career took him next, I would not be left behind. True to his word, when The Nation newspaper launched on July 31, 2006, I continued working with him as a 16-year-old boy. One quality that set him apart from the very beginning was his uncommon, almost instinctive generosity. I remember one particular week when he repeatedly asked whether I had eaten. Each time, he would give me some money for food. As time passed and his instinctive generosity continued, I grew uncomfortable and began answering, “Yes, sir, I have eaten,” not because I had suddenly become rich, but because I did not want him to think I was turning hunger into a business strategy. That is Mr. Omotoso. His kindness is never calculated; it flows naturally. His generosity was never limited to me. I recall a difficult period when the newspaper’s salaries were delayed for months. The newsroom was dampened, heavy with frustration. Sensing and discerning the quiet despair of his colleagues, he reached into his own pocket and gave everyone money to ease the hardship. That single gesture taught me a lesson I have never forgotten: true leadership is not about occupying an office; it is about lifting others when life weighs them down. Beyond feeding my body, Mr. Omotoso fed my dreams. He encouraged me to keep studying while working and never once treated my academic ambitions as an inconvenience. During one management meeting, when questions were raised about my qualifications, he defended my potential and appealed for patience while I worked toward becoming a graduate. I was determined not to disappoint him. In 2014, I graduated from the then Lagos State Polytechnic with a Distinction. He celebrated the achievement, then immediately urged me to aim higher. With his continued support, I went on to Caleb University, Imota, Lagos, where I earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Computer Science in 2019, graduating with Second Class Upper honours and a CGPA of 4.36. For someone who had started as an errand boy, this was more than academic progress. It was living proof that when someone believes in your potential, your circumstances need not determine your destination. Mr. Omotoso’s fatherly role extended far beyond the professional and academic. When I married in 2018, he provided a Honda Pilot and a personal driver to take me around all day, ensuring the occasion was memorable. On August 20, 2019, he was appointed Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy. Before leaving The Nation, he ensured my contributions were recognised with a promotion to Web Officer. A month into his new assignment, he invited me to join him at the Ministry of Information and Strategy. That invitation opened yet another significant chapter in my career. Since then, I have had the privilege of serving closely with him as his Personal Assistant and Programme Analyst within the Lagos State Government. His commitment to my progress did not end there. He played an instrumental role in my appointment to the Lagos State Civil Service on December 31, 2024, personally presenting my credentials to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for consideration and approval. How does one adequately thank a man who has consistently opened doors, sometimes long before one even knew those doors existed? Yet my story is only one among countless testimonies of his compassion. Over the years, I have watched him discreetly pay hospital bills for people with whom he shares no family ties, sponsor the education of children whose parents could not afford school fees, and quietly rescue others from difficult circumstances. He does not need a camera to demonstrate kindness, nor does he wait for applause before helping others. Behind his serious editorial background and the demands of public office is also a man blessed with a remarkable sense of humour. An accomplished journalist, columnist and writer, Mr. Omotoso has a gift for satire. His humorous observations can turn even tense moments into shared laughter. And then there is table tennis. Anyone who has faced him across the table knows that losing is not exactly his favourite pastime. He approaches every game with the intensity of an editor scrutinising a controversial front-page headline. Every point matters, every rally is a battle, and every defeat deserves a detailed explanation. At 65, I suspect his opponents will still need more than youthful energy to defeat him. As I celebrate this remarkable man, I see far beyond the professional titles and accomplishments. I see a compassionate father figure, a bridge-builder, a generous leader, and a man whose quiet influence continues to transform lives. Sir, on your 65th birthday, I pray that Almighty God grants you long life, sound health, renewed strength, divine protection, and enduring peace. May the years ahead be filled with greater accomplishments, happiness, and the joy of seeing the many lives you have touched continue to flourish. May God reward every sacrifice you have made for others, replenish every resource you have so freely and generously shared, and surround you with love, honour and abundant blessings. May your pen never run dry, your wisdom never diminish, your laughter never cease, and may you continue winning your table tennis matches, even when your opponents believe they deserve a chance! For more than 22 years, I have experienced your kindness firsthand. I may never be able to repay all you have done for me, but I will forever remain grateful. Happy 65th birthday, my boss, my mentor, my father figure, and my God-sent benefactor. The world may know you as Gbenga Omotoso, the accomplished journalist and Commissioner. I know you as the man God used to rewrite the story of a fatherless boy. And for that, I will remain eternally grateful. •Uwemedimo is a Programme Analyst and Personal Assistant to the Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy. The post Gbenga Omotoso at 65: A rare gift of generosity and mentorship appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Automobile : avec 159 MMDH d’exportations, le Maroc consolide son leadership industriel
items.description: Premier secteur exportateur du Royaume et du continent africain, l’industrie automobile confirme son poids dans l’économie marocaine. Avec 159 milliards de dirhams (MMDH) d’exportations et une contribution de 24 % à la valeur ajoutée industrielle, la filière aborde une nouvelle phase de développement, portée notamment par l’extension des capacités de production et les investissements dans les véhicules électriques et les batteries. L’industrie automobile s’impose plus que jamais comme l’un des principaux moteurs de l’économie marocaine. Avec 159 MMDH d’exportations, elle occupe désormais la première place parmi les secteurs exportateurs du Royaume, tout en consolidant sa position à l’échelle africaine. Cette progression repose sur le développement des capacités industrielles, l’amélioration de l’intégration locale et l’arrivée de nouveaux investissements dans les différentes composantes de la filière. Les données figurant dans les documents accompagnant le projet de loi de finances (PLF) 2027 mettent en évidence le poids croissant de cette industrie. Le secteur contribue à hauteur de 24 % à la valeur ajoutée industrielle nationale, tandis que son taux d’intégration locale avoisine les 70 %. Les indicateurs de 2026 confirment cette dynamique. À fin août, les ventes automobiles à l’étranger ont atteint 116,1 MMDH, en hausse de 14,5 % par rapport à la même période de l’année précédente. Le secteur représente ainsi 34,7 % des exportations marocaines, contre 32,9 % un an auparavant. À lui seul, il explique près de 54,7 % de la croissance globale des exportations. Renault et Stellantis renforcent leurs capacités de production Cette dynamique devrait se poursuivre à travers plusieurs projets industriels structurants. Parmi eux figure le plan de développement de Renault pour la période 2025/30, qui prévoit de porter la capacité de production à 500.000 véhicules par an et le taux d’intégration locale à environ 80%. Le programme couvre la production de véhicules thermiques, hybrides et électriques. Il prévoit également la création d’un centre d’ingénierie, de recherche et développement à Tanger, destiné à renforcer les compétences nationales dans les domaines de l’innovation et de l’ingénierie industrielle. Du côté de Stellantis, le projet d’extension de l’usine de Kénitra vise à porter sa capacité annuelle à 400.000 véhicules et 350.000 moteurs. Il comprend également le lancement de deux nouveaux modèles reposant sur la plateforme Smart Car. Ces investissements doivent contribuer à élargir le tissu industriel autour des constructeurs, notamment à travers le développement des fournisseurs locaux et la production de composants à plus forte valeur ajoutée. Les batteries électriques, nouveau relais de croissance L’un des axes majeurs de la stratégie industrielle présentée dans le cadre du PLF 2027 concerne le développement d’une filière intégrée de batteries pour véhicules électriques. Plusieurs investisseurs sont associés à cette dynamique, notamment Gotion High-Tech, COBCO, BTR et TINCI. Les documents accompagnant le projet de loi de finances font notamment état d’un projet de première gigafactory en Afrique, pour un investissement prévisionnel de 14 MMDH. L’ambition ne se limite pas à la fabrication de batteries. Les orientations annoncées portent sur la structuration de l’ensemble de la chaîne de valeur de la mobilité électrique, depuis les batteries et les minerais critiques jusqu’au recyclage, en passant par la production et l’assemblage de véhicules électriques. Le gouvernement prévoit également de poursuivre les projets d’investissement engagés dans ce domaine, notamment celui de BTR, ainsi que la montée en puissance progressive des capacités de production de Gotion High-Tech à l’horizon 2029. Une industrie tournée vers l’intégration locale et l’innovation Pour 2027, les priorités gouvernementales portent sur le renforcement de l’intégration locale dans plusieurs filières industrielles, dont l’automobile, l’aéronautique, le textile, l’agroalimentaire, la chimie, l’électricité et l’électronique. L’objectif consiste notamment à développer des écosystèmes industriels autour des grands projets d’investissement et à accroître la production nationale de composants, afin de renforcer la compétitivité des entreprises marocaines et de réduire la dépendance aux importations. La recherche et l’innovation figurent également parmi les leviers retenus. Le Fonds de soutien à l’innovation a financé 154 projets et mobilisé 826,26 millions de dirhams d’investissements dans la recherche, le développement et l’innovation industrielle. Le programme de développement de la recherche et de l’innovation industrielles a, par ailleurs, été prolongé de trois années supplémentaires, jusqu’en 2028. Son budget a été renforcé de 900 millions de dirhams, avec un objectif de 100 projets accompagnés chaque année. Cette orientation s’inscrit dans une stratégie visant à renforcer la souveraineté industrielle, à favoriser la substitution des importations par la production nationale et à réduire l’empreinte carbone des activités industrielles. Dans cette perspective, la mobilité électrique et sa chaîne de valeur sont appelées à occuper une place croissante dans le développement industriel du Maroc. La progression des exportations automobiles confirme le rôle central de cette filière dans les échanges extérieurs du Royaume. Le défi des prochaines années sera de transformer cette performance en davantage de valeur ajoutée locale, de compétences technologiques et d'activités industrielles maîtrisées sur le territoire national. The post Automobile : avec 159 MMDH d’exportations, le Maroc consolide son leadership industriel appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: 15e Symposium de sculpture sur granite de Laongo : les travaux officiellement lancés
items.description: La 15ᵉ édition du Symposium international de sculpture sur granite de Laongo a été officiellement lancée, le mercredi 11 novembre 2026. 20 artistes de plusieurs pays prennent part à cette rencontre placée sous le signe de la création, du dialogue interculturel et de la transmission des savoir-faire. Le granite reprend ses lettres de noblesse à Laongo. Depuis le mercredi 11 novembre 2026, des artistes venus de plusieurs pays ont investi le site pour donner forme à de nouvelles œuvres sculpturales, à l'occasion de la 15ᵉ édition du Symposium international de sculpture sur granite. Le lancement officiel des travaux a été marqué par les premiers coups de burin, donnés le mercredi 11 novembre 2026, par le ministre de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, Pingdwendé Gilbert Ouédraogo. P our cette édition, 20 sculpteurs professionnels venus du Burkina Faso, du Mali, du Niger, du Bénin, de la Turquie, de la Belgique, de l’Iran, du Sénégal, de la Chine, de l’Italie, du Kenya et de l’Inde sont réunis autour du granite. Du 9 au 23 novembre, ils vont confronter leurs expériences, leurs techniques et leurs imaginaires. L'objectif est de faire émerger de nouvelles œuvres inspirées des identités et des cultures des peuples. Pour le ministre de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, Pingdwendé Gilbert Ouédraogo, le symposium de Laongo est devenu un rendez-vous majeur de la création artistique et du dialogue interculturel. Au fil des éditions, il a contribué au développement d'une expertise burkinabè dans la sculpture et la taille du granite, a-t-il ajouté. Selon lui, les œuvres réalisées sur le site constituent aujourd'hui un patrimoine exceptionnel. Elles font de Laongo un véritable musée à ciel ouvert. « Laongo est désormais un patrimoine vivant, une vitrine de notre potentiel créatif et une contribution singulière de notre pays au patrimoine culturel universel », a souligné le ministre Ouédraogo. Au-delà de l'esthétique, le ministre chargé des Arts voit dans cette manifestation un instrument de transformation sociale. La culture participe à l'affirmation de l'identité, à la cohésion sociale et à la transmission des valeurs aux générations futures, a insisté Pingdwendé Gilbert Ouédraogo. La 15ᵉ édition s'articule autour de quatre principales activités. La première est le chantier-école. Il offre à 15 jeunes stagiaires une formation théorique et pratique aux techniques de sculpture et de taille sur granite. Cette initiative vise à assurer la transmission des savoir-faire et à préparer la relève. La deuxième activité est un colloque scientifique autour du thème : « La sculpture sur granite : expression et construction des identités culturelles ». Les échanges vont porter notamment sur la place de la création artistique dans la construction des identités, la préservation de la mémoire collective et la valorisation des patrimoines. Laongo, « une école supérieure d'art » La résidence de création constitue le cœur de la manifestation. Elle réunit les 20 artistes professionnels jusqu'au 23 novembre. La diversité de leurs origines devrait favoriser le partage d'expériences et le brassage des expressions artistiques. Enfin, la foire artistique et commerciale « Village Sympo Granite », prévue du 11 au 17 novembre, offre une vitrine aux créateurs et aux acteurs de la commercialisation des produits artistiques et culturels. Elle entend également promouvoir l'entrepreneuriat culturel. Parrain artistique de cette édition, l'artiste plasticien malien, Abdoulaye Konaté, a rappelé l'importance historique de la sculpture dans les sociétés africaines. Pour lui, cet art constitue une expression ancienne de la créativité humaine. Il a invité les jeunes à s'intéresser davantage à cette discipline et à en faire un véritable métier. « Laongo n'est pas seulement un centre touristique. Nous avons la chance que Laongo soit une école supérieure d'art au niveau du granite et du bronze », a-t-il affirmé. Il a estimé que le site représente une particularité pour le Burkina Faso, la Confédération des Etats du Sahel (AES) et l'Afrique. Le parrain artistique a également appelé à mieux valoriser les créateurs et les personnalités culturelles du Burkina Faso. Le pays dispose, selon lui, d'un potentiel artistique important qui mérite attention et accompagnement. En rendant hommage aux pionniers qui ont contribué à faire de Laongo un haut lieu de création, le ministre Ouédraogo a invité les artistes à inscrire dans le granite les aspirations des peuples et les valeurs à transmettre aux générations futures. Djakaridia SIRIBIE

items.title: Women and their househelps: The cruelty must stop
items.description: By Fred Chukwuelobe I don’t mind being called a misogynist or accused of generalising on this matter. Frankly, I think we have reached a point where somebody has to speak out loudly against the inhuman treatment some Igbo women mete out to their domestic servants. And while we are at it, we must also call out their husbands, particularly those who watch helplessly as their wives turn other people’s children into household slaves. Some of these men are either complicit or simply too weak to call their wives to order. For quite some time now, stories of Igbo women who mercilessly maltreat their domestic servants have been making the rounds. The latest is the disturbing incident in Ogidi, Anambra State, where a woman allegedly beat her 10-year-old domestic servant so mercilessly that a neighbour had to intervene to rescue the child. Reports identified the girl as Chizoba Ifeanyi and the alleged perpetrator as her aunt, Mrs Adaobi Agbonta. The incident reportedly occurred because the little girl refused to sweep the house. Imagine that! What manner of woman beats a ten-year-old child to that extent over an ordinary household chore? What exactly does she expect from a child of that age? And what would have happened if that neighbour had not intervened? Unfortunately, this is not the first time we have heard such stories. In July 2020, Nigerians were horrified by the story of 10-year-old Nneoma Nnadi in Enugu. Her employer, Ifeoma Ozougwu, was accused of inserting a six-inch nail into the child’s skull, using hot pressing irons on her body and subjecting her to other forms of torture. Her husband was also arrested in connection with the incident. It was one of those stories that made one wonder whether some people were actually human beings. In May 2023, another case emerged from Nkpor, Anambra State, involving an eight-year-old househelp who was allegedly brutally beaten by her employer, Chinyere Ifesinachi. The child reportedly sustained multiple injuries. Then there was the March 2018 case in Lagos involving a woman, Nkeiruka Ngwu, who was arrested for allegedly using a hot pressing iron and hot water on her 10-year-old househelp, Chioma Samuel, a child reportedly brought from Abia State after the death of her father. These are just some of the reported cases. And before anybody accuses me of deliberately picking on Igbo women, let me acknowledge that similar incidents have occurred in other parts of the country. In March 2026, Premium Times reported the arrest of a woman in Cross River State over the alleged assault of her five-year-old niece, who was reportedly being used as a domestic helper. In Delta State, a woman was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment in 2020 for using a hot kitchen knife to disfigure the mouth of her nine-year-old housemaid. I am not aware of any reliable national statistics establishing which ethnic group records the highest number of such abuses. But the frequency of disturbing stories involving women in our part of the country should worry us. We cannot continue pretending that nothing is happening. Thank goodness I am Igbo, so nobody should waste time accusing me of Igbophobia. I am talking about a problem that deserves to be confronted within our society. And I am certainly not suggesting that all Igbo women behave this way. Far from it. There are countless decent, compassionate and responsible Igbo women who treat their domestic workers with love and dignity. But those who engage in these atrocities must be called out. What exactly is the matter with some of these women? Why are they so wicked to other people’s children? These are children born to poor parents, just as their own children were born. Some have lost their parents. Others come from homes where their parents cannot afford to provide for them. They are sent to live with relatives or brought into households where they are expected to receive care, assistance and, in some cases, an opportunity to go to school. Instead, some end up living like slaves. They are made to wake up before everybody else, cook, wash, clean, fetch water, look after babies and perform virtually every household chore. They eat last, sleep last and are often the first to be blamed whenever anything goes wrong. Some are fed with leftovers or denied food altogether for the slightest offence. Others are denied access to education and decent clothing. Once you see some of these women and their children on an outing to events and even church services, you can easily identify the househelp. The difference in their dressing alone tells a story. The madam’s children are beautifully dressed, while the little girl or boy accompanying them looks like somebody picked up from the street. I recall seeing a woman who took her children to a fast-food restaurant. While the children sat comfortably at the table enjoying their lunch, their domestic servant sat somewhere nearby, clutching madam’s handbag and watching them eat. She was not even treated as someone who deserved to sit at the same table and enjoy a meal. I found the sight particularly disturbing. I also recall a case in which a woman allegedly used a hot pressing iron on her domestic servant because the child drank a soft drink meant for her own children. A bottle of soft drink! Can you imagine burning another person’s child because she drank what your children were meant to drink? What kind of wickedness is that? Some of these women apparently believe that because they provide accommodation and food for their domestic servants, they have acquired ownership of their lives. They forget that these children have parents, feelings, dignity and rights. Even if their parents are dead, they remain human beings deserving of compassion. And what is even more disturbing is that some of these women are regular churchgoers. They attend services, participate in church activities, make donations and sometimes occupy prominent positions in their religious organisations. On Sundays, they sing praises and pray fervently. But when they return home, the same hands that are raised in worship are used to beat and torment another person’s child. What manner of Christianity is that? Then there are the husbands. I have a special word for them. Some of you need to grow a backbone. How can you sit in your living room, know that your wife is beating and maltreating a little child, and pretend that nothing is happening? Is the child not a human being? Does your responsibility to protect the vulnerable end because the person abusing the child happens to be your wife? Marriage does not require you to surrender your conscience. If your wife is cruel to a domestic servant, call her to order. If she refuses to change, protect the child and involve the appropriate authorities. Do not become an accomplice simply because you want peace at home. I also have a word for the relatives who send their children away to live with wealthy relations. Please, do not abandon your parental responsibilities simply because somebody has promised to take care of your child. Visit. Call. Ask questions. Find out what the child eats, where the child sleeps and whether the child is attending school. Do not wait until the child returns home with scars or ends up in a hospital before you realise that something has gone terribly wrong. WE MUST DECLARE WAR ON THIS PRACTICE. I believe it is time for Igbo sociocultural organisations, town unions, women’s organisations, civil society groups and religious institutions to take this matter seriously. It should no longer be treated as an ordinary domestic disagreement. Where are our women organisations? Where are the church groups that organise meetings every week? Where are the Christian Mothers’ organisations? Where are the wives of our governors? Why should we wait until another child is nearly killed before everybody starts issuing statements? The First Ladies of the South-East states should take up this challenge and champion a regional campaign against the abuse of domestic workers. Traditional rulers, presidents-general of town unions and community leaders should make child protection a regular subject of discussion in their communities. Our governments must also wake up. The Child Rights Act and the corresponding state laws provide a legal framework for protecting children against abuse, exploitation and neglect. These laws must be enforced. Those found guilty of abusing children should face the full consequences of the law. We must stop the practice of settling serious cases of child abuse quietly within families or through some backdoor community arrangement. If existing laws are inadequate, the state legislatures should strengthen them. There should also be proper regulation of domestic-worker recruitment, particularly where children are involved. No child should be handed over to an employer under an arrangement that leaves the child without protection or accountability. Neighbours must also learn to intervene. If you hear a child screaming persistently or notice unexplained injuries, do not look the other way. Report the matter. You may be saving a child’s life. I am particularly concerned that the behaviour of these women is beginning to cast an unnecessary shadow on other Igbo women who are decent, responsible and compassionate towards their domestic workers. That is unfair to the many women who treat their househelps as human beings, provide for their education and give them opportunities they might otherwise not have had. But decent people must not remain silent while others behave like monsters. We must also stop pretending that every child brought into a home as a househelp is necessarily enjoying some form of privilege. In some cases, what is happening is nothing short of exploitation. A child who is denied education, adequate food, decent accommodation and basic human dignity, while being compelled to work from morning till night, is not enjoying the benefits of living with a wealthy family. That child is being exploited. Slavery ended centuries ago. It must not be surreptitiously reintroduced through the back door by women who believe that other people’s children are available for them to treat anyhow. I have said my piece. It is time for our communities, governments, religious institutions and, particularly, the womenfolk to rise against this barbaric practice. We cannot continue to look away while vulnerable children are subjected to indignity and cruelty in the very homes where they should be safe. A househelp is not a slave. A poor child is not a second-class human being. And no amount of wealth, marriage or social status can excuse cruelty. That is the message we must send, loudly and unequivocally. •Chukwuelobe wrote in from Lagos. The post Women and their househelps: The cruelty must stop appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Patronise indigenous firms to create jobs, boost development, Ifezue tells S’East govs
items.description: By Chimaobi Nwaiwu NNEWI — South-East governors have been urged to support and patronise factories and companies established by indigenes of the zone to generate employment, tackle insecurity and unemployment, and accelerate regional development. The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Audi Company Limited, Dr Clem Ifezue, made the call in an exclusive interview with Vanguard in Awka, Anambra State. Ifezue, an Anambra-born industrialist, said indigenous industries had the capacity to provide jobs for thousands of unemployed people and contribute significantly to the economic growth of the South-East if given adequate government support and patronage. He said Audi Company Limited was a technical products and services marketing company registered in Nigeria, with a vision to assemble leading global brands and make them readily available to Nigerians. According to him, the company has been operating for over 20 years, with branches across the country’s regions, including Enugu, and partnerships with several local and international companies. Highlighting areas where South-East governors could partner with the company, Ifezue said its operations covered automobile assembly, power solutions, marine logistics and engineering works. He explained that the company’s power solutions included generators powered by Perkins and York engines of British origin, as well as solar systems, hybrid inverters, lithium batteries and solar panels. “When I say power solution, it means that we have our own brand of generators, using Perkins and York engines, both of United Kingdom origin. “We have been in existence for a while and Nigerians have been enjoying the quality of our products and can attest to that. “We have our own brand of solar system, we have our inverter which is hybrid, we have our battery which is lithium and we have our solar panels, with well-trained engineers and technicians working for us. We are a big employer of labour,” he said. On marine logistics, Ifezue said the company had partnerships in boat construction and the provision of marine facilities for transportation, fishing and movement of goods, among other applications. He also disclosed that the company was involved in engineering and construction projects for state governments and private individuals. Ifezue, who is also the Director-General of the Mines Crafts Registered Association of Nigeria, said South-East governors could leverage the company’s expertise to attract investments and accelerate infrastructure development in the region. The former General Manager of John Holt Plc lamented the difficulties of establishing and sustaining businesses in Nigeria, attributing some of the challenges to what he described as inadequate government emphasis on supporting indigenous enterprises. He said local companies often competed with foreign operators who had limited investments and business establishments in Nigeria but were still able to secure contracts and patronage. “We compete with a lot of people who do not have anything here in Nigeria, people who just come with one briefcase, do business and go, but we are established here. “That is why we said we represent the best brands. Together with Mikano Motors, we assemble cars, sell and maintain the cars in Nigeria,” he said. He acknowledged the Federal Government’s efforts to reduce high bank interest rates, but argued that more deliberate policies were needed to enable indigenous companies to compete effectively and provide quality products at affordable prices. According to him, government remains the biggest spender in Nigeria through its activities at the federal, state and local government levels and could significantly influence the growth of local industries through its procurement decisions. He cited the purchase of official vehicles, equipment for government agencies and vehicles for public officers as areas where governments could patronise locally assembled products. Ifezue also referenced the Ebonyi State Government’s provision of vehicles to doctors serving in rural communities as an example of how government procurement could support public service delivery and local businesses. “If government is sincere with their preaching of patronising Made-in-Nigeria goods, it will be a good thing for the economy. “It is by so doing that our competitors will begin to think of setting up plants here, but as far as the government is ignoring indigenous companies and patronising those that are not established here, that campaign will not be successful,” he said. He urged governments at all levels to extend their patronage beyond automobile assembly plants to other products manufactured locally, arguing that such a policy would stimulate investment, create employment and strengthen the economy. Ifezue expressed optimism that a coordinated partnership between South-East governors and indigenous businesses would encourage more investors to establish factories in the region. “If the South-East governors can come together and form an alliance with us, more industries will be attracted and located here, our people will be employed and more development will come. “Location of industries goes with numbers. If we are assured of high patronage, more people will set up factories and our people stand to gain. No investor will like to invest where he cannot make a profit,” he said. The post Patronise indigenous firms to create jobs, boost development, Ifezue tells S’East govs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Right-sizing the map of Africa
items.description: The United Nations General Assembly has, for the first time, formally endorsed a global shift away from the centuries-old Mercator map in favour of projections that show Africa—and other equatorial regions—in their true relative size. This “Correct the Map” resolution, spearheaded by Togo on behalf of the African Group and backed by the African Union, passed by 164 votes to one, with six abstentions. While non-binding, it marks a watershed moment in how the world visually represents the continent—and, by extension, how it perceives Africa’s weight in global affairs. The root of the misrepresentation lies in the Mercator projection, devised in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator for maritime navigation. To keep compass bearings straight, Mercator preserved angles and shapes—but at the cost of area. The result: landmasses near the poles, such as Europe, North America and Greenland, are visually enlarged, while those near the equator, including Africa, Latin America and South Asia, are shrunk. On typical Mercator wall maps, Greenland appears roughly the same size as Africa. In reality, Africa covers about 30.3 million square kilometres, making it around 14 times larger than Greenland’s 2.1 million square kilometres. This is not a minor quirk; it is a systematic visual bias baked into the most widely used world map for nearly five centuries. The resolution encourages governments, schools, international organisations, media houses and technology companies to adopt equal-area projections, especially the Equal Earth projection, whenever comparative continental size matters. It frames map distortion as more than a technical issue—calling it a cognitive, educational, cultural and geopolitical problem that has contributed to the symbolic minimisation of Africa in the global imagination. While symbolic correction matters, Africa’s greatest vulnerabilities lie in structural exploitation and escalating insecurity, notably from Islamist insurgencies across the Sahel, Lake Chad Basin and parts of the Horn. Map reform must be paired with hard-edged action on multiple fronts. First, curb external exploitation and illicit financial flows by tightening transparency on extractives, choking illicit financial flows through cross-border tax cooperation, and rebalancing investment terms to prioritise local content and value addition. Second, confront Islamist insecurity with a whole-of-system approach by funding and professionalising regional forces, targeting financing networks that fuel insurgencies, investing in governance at the frontier, and countering extremist narratives through community engagement. Third, lock in development dividends that undercut recruitment by expanding vocational training and agro-processing corridors tied to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), funding climate-resilient livelihoods, and prioritising children’s education and primary healthcare. Fourth, reform global governance to reflect Africa’s weight by pressing for permanent African seats at the UN Security Council. The UN’s “Correct the Map” resolution is a necessary correction of a 450-year-old visual injustice. But maps alone do not feed children, stop bullets or reclaim stolen wealth. The post Right-sizing the map of Africa appeared first on Vanguard News .
