items.title: Accra after Sunset: El Niño, a heating city and the sky above us
items.description: By Petras Anaab Ali (MPhil) The sun has gone down, but the room still feels hot. The fan is running, yet sleep does not come easily. Outside, people seek relief on verandas, in compound yards and along the roadside. For anyone who has spent such an evening in Accra, the question is simple: why does sunset bring so little comfort? That question has become more urgent. On 30 October 2026, the Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) warned that a very strong and still intensifying El Niño is developing, and that Ghana should prepare for a hotter, drier and dustier dry season. Heat stress is expected to peak between February and April 2027, especially in the north. The ocean data behind that warning are striking. In mid-October, the weekly Niño 3.4 index, the standard measure of El Niño, reached +3.3°C . Scientists classify anything above +2.0°C as “very strong.” For Accra, the warning raises a practical question: how prepared is a densely built city for additional heat? Answering it means looking at three things together: the global climate, the city we have built, and, less obviously, the whole column of atmosphere above us. My MPhil research in Physics at the University of Ghana followed the last strong El Niño upwards through that column. What it found is that El Niño does not only change the weather at ground level. It disturbs the entire sky. A distant ocean, a connected atmosphere El Niño begins with unusually warm surface water in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. Normally, trade winds push warm water westward towards Asia. During El Niño those winds weaken, and the warm pool spreads east. Warm water heats the air above it, the air rises, and storm clouds form where they normally would not. That shift in where the atmosphere draws its heat rearranges winds and rainfall across the globe. Scientists call these long-distance links teleconnections. El Niño strength Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly Weak +0.5°C to +0.9°C Moderate +1.0°C to +1.4°C Strong +1.5°C to +1.9°C Very strong +2.0°C or higher The present event is far beyond the top of that scale. In September, the US Climate Prediction Center put the chance at 75% that it would exceed every El Niño recorded since 1950. The great events of 1982/83, 1997/98 and 2015/16 are remembered in Ghana for drought and bushfires, and the first two were followed by power rationing. Two cautions belong here, because they keep the argument honest. First, El Niño changes the odds; it does not dictate the weather of every community. Ghana’s seasons also depend on the tropical Atlantic, and GMet notes that a cool Gulf of Guinea could shape how the 2027 rains behave. Second, the heat people feel today cannot automatically be blamed on a forecast for the coming months. Establishing how unusual Accra’s present heat is requires local observations compared with the same season in earlier years. The planet is already running hot According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), September 2026 was the second-warmest September on record , with the global surface temperature 1.33°C above average . NOAA’s map for that month shows a bright red tongue of warm water stretching along the equator from South America across the Pacific: El Niño itself. Northern Canada and Siberia are deep red. Cooler-than-normal blue is now confined mostly to Antarctica and a few small patches. Ghana and the Gulf of Guinea appear in light pink, roughly half a degree to one degree above normal. That should not reassure us. Global temperatures usually peak a few months after El Niño itself peaks, because the heat released by the Pacific takes time to spread through the atmosphere. That is what happened after the 2023/24 El Niño, when 2024 went on to break global temperature records. On the evidence so far, West Africa’s turn is still coming. Accra already has a heat problem El Niño will not arrive in a cool city. Local evidence over the past year gives the discussion a firm foundation. Surfaces have heated sharply: A peer-reviewed study of the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area found that urban land surface temperature rose by an average of 4.07°C between 1991 and 2020 , as built-up land grew from about 31% to 73% of the area and forest cover fell from about 21% to 11%. Heat is now on the city’s agenda: In October 2025, the Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) trained 30 data collectors to survey households, hawkers and outdoor workers in heat-vulnerable zones including Chorkor, Mamprobi, Korle Gonno, Kaneshie, Makola, Agbogbloshie, Old Fadama and Jamestown, to inform the city’s first operational Heat Action Plan. Vulnerability is rising: In December 2025, AMA reported preliminary findings from its Urban Heat Vulnerability Assessment showing a sharp rise in land surface temperatures over three decades. The lead researcher said Accra is “heating faster than many imagine.” No neighborhood is spared: A study presented in June 2026 found rising heat in low-, middle- and high-income communities alike, from East Legon and Cantonments to Chorkor and Abossey Okai. It found women more affected than men, and, perhaps surprisingly, indoor workers more vulnerable than outdoor workers . One clarification matters. Land surface temperature is the temperature of roofs, roads and soil as seen by satellites. A 4°C rise in surface temperature does not mean the air everywhere in Accra has warmed by 4°C. But hot surfaces are exactly what keep a city warm after dark, which brings us back to that sleepless evening. Why sunset brings little relief The physics begins with the energy received during the day. Sunlight heats roofs, roads and walls. Dark surfaces absorb more of it, and dense materials such as concrete and block store it. After sunset, that stored energy keeps flowing into the surrounding air and into rooms, partly as infrared radiation we cannot see but can certainly feel. A room can stay uncomfortable long after the sun has gone because it is still releasing the day’s heat. How fast that heat escapes depend on ventilation, shade, roof design and how closely buildings are packed. Iron roofing sheets heat quickly under the sun; poorly ventilated rooms hold heat in. Trees and wetlands work the other way: they shade surfaces and cool the air through evaporation. As Accra has replaced vegetation with concrete, it has removed some of its own natural cooling. Humidity adds another layer. Our bodies cool mainly by evaporating sweat. In Accra’s humid coastal air, sweat evaporates slowly, so a night at 27°C can feel far more oppressive than the number suggests. A thermometer reading alone cannot describe the experience of heat. Who can afford relief? Heat is shared, but the ability to escape it is not. One household can run an air conditioner all night. Another depends on a single fan in a poorly ventilated room. A trader may have to stay at a roadside stall through the hottest hours because leaving means losing income. That helps explain why indoor workers in crowded, unventilated spaces can be more exposed than people working outside. Accra’s authorities have begun to document this. AMA’s citywide Extreme Heat Perceptions Survey asks residents how heat affects their health, livelihoods, productivity, sleep, transport and daily routines. It complements a heat-mapping exercise in which temperature sensors were installed across the city to identify hotspots. Publishing those results in an accessible form would let residents understand their own exposure and let the public judge whether interventions reach the places of greatest need. Electricity sits at the centre of this. Every fan and air conditioner draws power, and a hotter dry season will push demand up. The supply side carries its own El Niño risk. GMet says Lake Volta is in good shape for now, but warns that the real risk falls on the 2027 rainy season, which determines how much water will be available for hydropower in 2028. When power fails on a hot night, the fan stops, and the people with the fewest alternatives suffer most. Following the last El Niño upwards The heat we feel is only the bottom of the story. For my MPhil thesis, Investigation of the Potential Changes in Ionospheric Patterns Due to Climate Variability (University of Ghana, 2024), I compared the strong La Niña of 2020/21 with the strong El Niño of 2023/24. I used temperature profiles from the COSMIC-2 satellites, covering the atmosphere from the ground to 60 km, and navigation-satellite signals recorded in Bogotá (Colombia), Antananarivo (Madagascar) and Baie-Comeau (Canada). Those signals reveal the Total Electron Content (TEC) of the ionosphere, the electrically charged layer roughly 100 to 1,000 km up that every GPS signal must cross. To be clear, that work did not measure temperatures in Accra’s streets or homes. But it showed that El Niño leaves a fingerprint at every level of the atmosphere. Layer What was measured La Niña (2020/21) El Niño (2023/24) Lower atmosphere (2–5 km) Strength of early-morning temperature inversion 5–8 K 3–5 K Lower atmosphere Time the morning inversion breaks up Baseline 30–45 minutes earlier Upper troposphere Size of wave-driven temperature disturbances 1–2 K 3–4 K Stratosphere (20–30 km) Tropical stratospheric temperature Baseline About 2–3 K warmer Ionosphere Irregularity in electron content 1.7–2.1 TECU 2.4–2.8 TECU (25–40% higher) Ionosphere Night-time electron content Baseline 30–40% higher In plain terms: during El Niño, the stable morning layer of air that acts as a lid on the lower atmosphere was weaker and broke up earlier, so convection started sooner and reached higher. That churning launches atmospheric gravity waves, ripples in the air that grow as they climb into thinner air, much as a whip’s crack builds towards its tip. A warmer stratosphere let more of those waves through, and when they reached the ionosphere, they stirred up its charged gas. The Sun is the ionosphere’s main driver, so the two had to be separated. My La Niña year fell near solar minimum and my El Niño year near solar maximum. After statistically removing solar activity, El Niño still explained an additional 17–27% of the variation in the ionosphere’s electron content . The study was among the first systematic analyses of El Niño’s effect on the African equatorial ionosphere, and the African station responded as strongly as stations elsewhere in the tropics. The Sun has been active this season too. The provisional Dst index, which tracks geomagnetic storms, recorded six disturbances between September and October 2026. The strongest, on 11 October, reached about −93 nanotesla , a moderate storm just short of the intense threshold. My thesis concluded that El Niño-linked ionospheric variability can rival a moderate geomagnetic storm of that kind. The difference is duration: a solar storm passes in a day or two, while El Niño’s influence persists for months. Why should anyone in Accra care? Because a disturbed ionosphere bends and delays satellite signals. My analysis suggests El Niño-linked changes can produce position errors of a meter or more, and vertical errors of 2 to 3 meters for single-frequency receivers , the kind found in most everyday devices. That will not stop anyone finding a trotro station, but it matters for satellite-guided aircraft approaches, land surveying, precision farming, drones and radio communications. West Africa sits beneath the equatorial ionization anomaly, one of the most turbulent parts of the ionosphere, where irregularities after sunset are already common. My data showed night-time electron content rising 30 to 40% during El Niño, precisely when those irregularities are worst. I must add one honest note. None of my stations was in Ghana, because long, continuous, publicly available records of the kind this study needed were not available here. A Ghanaian physicist studying the African sky had to use data from Madagascar. What the next set of numbers should show Good decisions need better local data. Four things would sharpen the picture considerably: Night-time temperatures: Daily minimum temperatures are a good start. Hourly records would show how quickly Accra cools after sunset and how long uncomfortable conditions last. Fair comparisons: This season’s readings should be compared with the same calendar period in earlier years, including past El Niño dry seasons (1997/98, 2015/16, 2023/24) and neutral years. Otherwise, normal seasonal change can be mistaken for exceptional warming. Humidity and neighborhood context: Humidity should be reported alongside temperature, and comparisons between neighborhoods should account for trees, building density and distance from the coast. More than one El Niño: My own thesis compared a single El Niño with a single La Niña. Any firm conclusion about El Niño and Ghana should cover several events and account for the long-term warming trend. The purpose is to give residents a clear account of what is changing, where exposure is greatest, and which responses the evidence justifies. Turning warnings into cooler places There is a foundation to build on. In April 2026, the Mayor of Accra announced plans to amend AMA’s bye-laws to formally recognize heat as a public health risk, after a review found major gaps in how the city handles extreme heat. The new provisions are to focus on markets, transport terminals and temporary structures. AMA’s public health leadership has also called for reforms covering ventilation standards, roofing requirements, shade and green infrastructure. The task now is delivery. I would urge the following: Set up GMet’s proposed National El Niño and Dry-Season Preparedness Task Force without delay. GMet recommends one bringing together the relevant ministries, the Volta River Authority and local government, reporting monthly to Cabinet. The peak heat period is weeks away. Get heat advisories into homes and workplaces, not only onto websites. Use radio, churches, mosques, markets and SMS, and name practical steps: drink water often, avoid strenuous activity in the hottest hours, and check on older people, young children and the sick. Make the bye-law reforms visible. Shaded waiting areas at lorry stations, cooler market spaces and better-ventilated buildings are outcomes residents can see and judge. Plant trees that survive. Tree planting must come with maintenance budgets and evidence that the trees are alive where shade is needed. Plan electricity for 2028, not only 2027. The Volta River Authority and the Energy Commission should model cooling demand now and prepare for weaker inflows into Lake Volta next year. Measure our own sky. As my thesis recommended, a network of dual-frequency satellite receivers across Africa, with Ghanaian universities and GMet as partners, would let us monitor the ionosphere ourselves, and a West African space weather advisory service would warn aviation, surveyors and farmers when it is disturbed. Africa needs to study Africa. The atmosphere does not stop at the top of the clouds, and neither should our science. One atmosphere, from our bedrooms to space The warm room after sunset and the disturbed ionosphere 300 km overhead are not separate stories. They are the same atmosphere responding to the same warm ocean. The data are clear: a Pacific running more than 3°C above normal, a planet in its second-warmest September on record, a city whose surfaces have heated by about 4°C in three decades, and a measurable El Niño fingerprint from the lowest kilometers of air to the top of the ionosphere. We cannot stop El Niño, but we can measure it, forecast it and prepare for it. GMet’s warning gives Ghana a few months before the peak heat arrives. The sun will keep setting over Accra. Whether its residents find relief afterwards depends partly on decisions we make before the next hot day begins. About the Author Petras Anaab Ali Petras Anaab Ali (MPhil), also known as Sumaila Ali or Coach Ali (The Supreme Tactician), holds a BSc and MPhil in Physics from the University of Ghana and is reading a certificate program in Biblical Studies at Heritage Bible Institute. His MPhil research investigated how El Niño and other forms of climate variability affect the ionosphere. His academic interests lie at the intersection of cosmology, quantum theory, philosophy of science and Christian theology. He works with Ghana’s Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) as a Programme Officer, contributing to environmental regulation and sustainability efforts. He is also a Sports Analyst, Researcher, Writer and Commentator with Radio Univers and Legon Today. LinkedIn: www.linkedin.com/in/petras-anaab-ali-mphil-5703553a6 Email: petrasanaabali@gmail.com

items.title: Tinubu recycling failed 2023 promises in 2027 manifesto, says ADC
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The African Democratic Congress, ADC, has accused President Bola Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress, APC, of recycling unfulfilled 2023 campaign promises in their newly unveiled 2027 manifesto, challenging the President to account for his record before seeking another mandate. The party said the manifesto reads like the programme of a political party seeking power for the first time, rather than that of a government that has controlled the Federal Government for nearly 12 years and has had more than three years under Tinubu to deliver on its promises. In a statement by its National Publicity Secretary, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the ADC cited healthcare coverage, ICT job creation and electricity generation as examples of promises it said the administration had failed to fulfil, questioning why Nigerians should be asked to embrace another set of commitments without an account of the previous ones. “The fundamental question Nigerians must ask is simple: Why is a government campaigning on promises it should already have fulfilled? President Tinubu has been in office since May 2023. The APC has controlled the Federal Government for nearly twelve years. Yet, reading this manifesto, one would think they are only now discovering the problems they were elected to solve,” the ADC said. The party recalled that Tinubu had promised in 2023 to extend health insurance coverage to 40 per cent of Nigerians within two years and create one million ICT jobs within 24 months. It claimed that barely one in ten Nigerians was now covered by health insurance, while government figures indicated that only about 15,000 jobs and opportunity pathways had been recorded, with the health insurance target shifted to 2031. The ADC also questioned the administration’s electricity performance, pointing out that the APC had described 4,500 megawatts of power generation as a crisis in 2023, only for its new manifesto to acknowledge average generation of 4,022 megawatts. “How does a government campaign to solve a crisis it has made remarkably worse?” the party queried. The opposition party further faulted Tinubu’s promise to introduce a programme for his first 100 days after re-election, arguing that the President already had the executive powers to implement the proposed measures without waiting for another electoral victory. “Most astonishingly, President Tinubu now promises a programme for his first 100 days after re-election, including measures he already possesses the executive powers to implement right now. What exactly is stopping him from acting today? What stopped him from acting in 2023 when he came into office?” the ADC asked. On the economy, the party accused the President of seeking another mandate without addressing the hardship confronting millions of households, claiming that poverty had risen to 63 per cent and the N70,000 minimum wage had lost more than a quarter of its purchasing power. “Yet, rather than account for the hardship he has inflicted on Nigerians and his long catalogue of failures across the economy and security sectors, the president and his party have the temerity to present another colourful brochure full of the same undelivered promises,” the statement said. The ADC insisted that campaign promises could no longer substitute for an assessment of the administration’s performance. “A manifesto is a promise of what a party will do. A record is evidence of what it has done. After eleven years, the APC cannot keep presenting promises as a substitute for performance,” it declared. It challenged Tinubu to publish a comprehensive account of his 2023 commitments, detailing what he had delivered, what remained unfulfilled and why the deadlines were missed, rather than shifting targets and repackaging old promises. The party said the 2027 election would be a referendum on Tinubu’s performance since assuming office, not an opportunity for him to present his presidency as though it were just beginning. “The President must understand that 2027 is first a referendum on his abysmal record since 2023, not an opportunity to pretend that his presidency is just about to begin. Nigeria needs a change of government, not another change of slogans,” the ADC declared.Police avert communal crisis as youths clash over colleague’s death in Kaduna By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo The Kaduna State Police Command has averted a possible communal crisis following a clash between rival youth groups from Kwaru and Unguwar Yero communities in Kaduna North Local Government Area of the state. The incident, which reportedly left some people injured, occurred on Wednesday morning following tension over the death of a youth who sustained injuries during an earlier confrontation between young people from the two communities. The deceased, reportedly from Unguwar Yero, was said to have died from injuries sustained during the disagreement about a week ago, triggering anger among his friends, who allegedly attempted to avenge his death on Wednesday. The development caused panic among residents, with some schoolchildren reportedly fleeing their schools as rival groups engaged in stone-throwing and other acts of violence. A resident of Kwaru, who identified himself as Sule, said the incident occurred around 9am when he heard noise and came out to see youths throwing stones at one another. “Some youths from Kwaru and Unguwar Yero had a disagreement about a week ago, during which a young man was injured and later died. “On Wednesday, after the children had gone to school, we started hearing noise. When I came out, I saw people gathering, while some were throwing stones at one another between the youths from Unguwar Yero and some residents of Kwaru who had gone to the cemetery,” he said. Sule said the incident heightened tension in the area, recalling that the two communities had experienced similar disagreements in the past before relative peace was restored. He confirmed that operatives of the Department of State Services (DSS), police and Mobile Police (MOPOL), among other security personnel, were deployed to the area to prevent further escalation and restore normalcy. Another resident, Mohammed, expressed concern over recurring disagreements among young people from the two communities. He said many of the youths were friends who often gathered together, adding that it was unfortunate that disagreements between them were sometimes given ethnic or religious interpretations. “They are youths who are friends, but whenever there is a disagreement among them, some people try to turn it into an ethnic or religious issue. That is not right,” he said. A teacher in the area, Bashir, also confirmed that three youths sustained injuries during the earlier confrontation, adding that one of them later died. He, however, said normal activities had started returning to the communities following the deployment of security personnel. There were also indications that the tension threatened to spread to neighbouring communities before security operatives intervened. The Kaduna State Police Command spokesman, DSP Mansir Hassan, confirmed the incident, saying the situation had been brought under control following the deployment of security personnel. “The situation is under control following a massive deployment of security personnel to the communities,” he said. The police intervention prevented the disagreement from degenerating into a wider security crisis, even as residents called for sustained security presence and peaceful engagement among youths and community stakeholders to forestall further violence. It was not confirmed as of the time of filing this report whether a curfew had been imposed on the affected communities. The post Tinubu recycling failed 2023 promises in 2027 manifesto, says ADC appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Indonesia: US Aid Cuts Fuel HIV
items.description: Click to expand Image An activist attends a vigil to mark World Aids Day in Jakarta, Indonesia, December 1, 2021. © 2021 Afriadi Hikmal/NurPhoto via AP US foreign aid cuts in 2025 abruptly ended essential community-based HIV prevention and care for LGBT people in Indonesia, who already face discrimination and arbitrary arrest.Dismantling of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) eliminated services for people at greatest risk of HIV, creating additional barriers to testing, prevention, and lifesaving treatment.Indonesia and international donors should restore care before more people are pushed out of treatment, more people die from preventable causes, and decades of progress against HIV is lost. (Jakarta) – United States foreign aid cuts in 2025 abruptly ended essential community-based HIV prevention and care for lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people in Indonesia who already face discrimination and arbitrary arrest, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. Globally, more than 170,000 additional people are estimated to have died in one year because of the cuts to HIV/AIDS response, which especially affect populations at increased risk of HIV infection. The 33-page report, “‘We Want to Be Treated as Human’: Impact of US Foreign Aid Cuts on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Care in Indonesia,” documents the Trump administration’s dismantling of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and finds that it eliminated services for people at greatest risk of HIV, creating additional barriers to testing, prevention, and lifesaving treatment. The Indonesian government and international donors should urgently restore support for community-led HIV/AIDS services. November 11, 2026 “We Want to be Treated as Human” Impact of US Foreign Aid Cuts on HIV/AIDS Prevention and Care in Indonesia Download the full report in English Annex I: Human Rights Watch Letter to the Indonesia Ministry of Health Annex II: Human Rights Watch Letter to the Indonesia Ministry of Home Affairs Annex III: Human Rights Watch Letter to the US Department of State “The Trump administration’s gutting of USAID eliminated services that helped LGBT people in Indonesia get lifesaving services in an environment of stigma, discrimination, and fear,” said Julia Bleckner, senior health researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Indonesia and international donors should restore care before more people are pushed out of treatment, more people die from preventable causes, and decades of progress against HIV is lost.” Human Rights Watch interviewed 35 people living with HIV, outreach workers, activists, academics, aid recipients, and staff of nongovernmental organizations in Jakarta, Depok, and Serang in November 2025 and June 2026, and reviewed budget and policy documents. Human Rights Watch wrote to the US Department of State and to the Indonesian Department of Health and the Ministry of Home Affairs on September 24, 2026, regarding the impact of the cuts, but has received no responses. The US government’s foreign assistance tracking website states that obligated funds for HIV in Indonesia dropped from $11.9 million in fiscal year 2024 to $7.9 million in FY25. These cuts included all USAID-funded community-based prevention and care directed to LGBT populations. Indonesia’s HIV/AIDS epidemic is concentrated among populations that face severe barriers to care due to discrimination and stigma. HIV prevalence is about 0.4 percent among the general population, compared with 22 percent among men who have sex with men and 25 percent among transgender people. Yet the most recent comprehensive spending data show that in 2020 only 0.1 percent of Indonesia’s domestic HIV/AIDS spending went to programs for men who have sex with men, and none went specifically to transgender people. International donors covered 98 percent of HIV programming for these populations, who frequently rely on community-led and outreach services due to the discrimination and stigma they encounter in public health facilities. Outreach workers had distributed condoms and information about preexposure prophylaxis, helped people obtain confidential testing, accompanied clients to clinics, and supported adherence to antiretroviral treatment. They also paid for transportation and tests, advocated for these patients with clinic staff, and trained health workers to provide respectful care. Outreach workers said that since the cuts they had lost contact with clients, that some clients were late collecting medication or missing doses, and that local organizations no longer had the capacity to track new infections and treatment interruptions. “Just leaving the house as a trans person is scary,” said a transgender outreach worker living with HIV. “Without an outreach worker, the person will be alone and they won’t get care.” The loss of services coincided with the Indonesian government's increasing attempts to criminalize and target at-risk groups. Indonesia’s new criminal code, which took effect on January 1, 2026, makes all consensual sex outside heterosexual marriage a criminal offense subject to complaints by close family members, effectively criminalizing same-sex conduct for the first time. Police raid private gatherings and have used possession of condoms and purported HIV medication as evidence of crimes. These practices deter people from carrying prevention supplies, gathering for outreach, testing for HIV, and seeking treatment. Transgender people whose identity documents do not reflect their gender identity may be publicly called by a former name, opening them up to humiliation or discrimination. Outreach workers have accompanied patients, advocated respectful treatment, helped people obtain identification and health insurance, and trained clinic staff. With funding gone, many people must now navigate these obstacles alone. A gay activist living with HIV spoke about the severity of the crisis: “If you are LGBT and living with HIV, it’s the end of the story. You are doomed.” After the US funding cuts, several governments quickly followed with their own. France, Japan, Germany, and others withdrew from financing the HIV/AIDS response. In June, Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the United Nations organization UNAIDS, said of the global funding cuts: “There’s no question that this is the most serious disruption in the HIV response since the world came together to fight this disease.” The Indonesian government should adequately fund HIV prevention and care for men who have sex with men and transgender people, support community-led organizations, ensure consistent supplies of antiretroviral medicines, and train health workers to provide nondiscriminatory care. The government should also repeal discriminatory laws, end unlawful raids targeting LGBT people, stop using possession of condoms and HIV medication as evidence of crimes, investigate and appropriately punish abuses by the police, and protect LGBT people from vigilante violence. The US government should ensure continuity and timely release of funding for the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) created in 2003, disclose the impact of terminated programs, and withdraw its “Promoting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance Policy,” which restricts work to protect the rights of transgender people and other issues. International donors should increase contributions to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria and directly support LGBT-led community organizations responding to HIV in Indonesia. “Indonesia should stop targeting LGBT people and start investing in the community services proven to prevent HIV and keep people in treatment,” Bleckner said. “The United States and other donors should help rebuild these lifelines, not abandon the people who depend on them.”

items.title: An II de la Confédération : la feuille de route en examen à Ouagadougou
items.description: Le ministre d’Etat, ministre de la Guerre et de la Défense patriotique, le général de division, Célestin Simporé, a présidé la cérémonie d’ouverture de la session confédérale du Conseil des ministres le mercredi 11 novembre 2026, à Ouagadougou. En prélude à la prochaine session du Collège des chefs d’Etat de la Confédération des Etats du Sahel (AES), une session confédérale du Conseil des ministres se tient les 11 et 12 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou. La cérémonie d’ouverture a été présidée par le ministre d’Etat, ministre de la Guerre et de la Défense patriotique, le général de division, Célestin Simporé. La rencontre vise à examiner la mise en œuvre de la feuille de route de l’An II de la confédération. A l’ouverture des travaux, le ministre d’Etat, Célestin Simporé, a appelé à consolider les acquis de l’organisation autour de ses trois piliers fondamentaux que sont la défense, la diplomatie et le développement. Il a exprimé sa satisfaction d’accueillir les délégations sœurs du Mali et du Niger. « Votre présence témoigne de la vitalité de notre Alliance et de notre engagement inébranlable à bâtir, ensemble, un avenir souverain et prospère pour nos laborieuses populations », a-t-il déclaré. Il a également rendu hommage aux trois chefs d’Etat membres de la Confédération, le général d’armée Assimi Goïta, le général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani et le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, Président du Faso et président de la Confédération. Saluant leur vision, il a estimé que leur engagement a permis de poser les bases d’une nouvelle dynamique politique et stratégique dans la sous-région. « Face aux soubresauts de l’histoire et aux menaces existentielles qui pesaient sur notre sous-région, ils ont fait le choix courageux de la rupture et de l’union sacrée », a-t-il souligné. Trois piliers au cœur de la feuille de route Revenant sur la feuille de route de l’An II, finalisée le 26 février 2026 à Ouagadougou, il a rappelé qu’elle s’inscrit dans une perspective de consolidation de la Confédération et de montée en puissance de l’espace AES. Les travaux de la session doivent ainsi permettre de faire le bilan des activités réalisées dans les trois domaines prioritaires. Sur le plan de la défense, il a insisté sur la nécessité de renforcer la coopération entre les forces armées des trois pays face à la menace terroriste. Il a notamment plaidé pour une harmonisation des outils, une meilleure mutualisation des renseignements et un renforcement de l’autonomie stratégique. En matière de diplomatie, le ministre Simporé a mis en avant la volonté des Etats membres de défendre collectivement leurs intérêts sur la scène internationale. « En portant nos idéaux d’une seule voix, nous redéfinissons nos partenariats et les diversifions sur la base stricte de nos intérêts nationaux et confédéraux gouvernés par les aspirations de nos peuples », a-t-il indiqué. Le troisième pilier, consacré au développement, vise à renforcer l’intégration économique des pays membres. Pour le ministre, la sécurité et la diplomatie ne sauraient prospérer sans un développement économique inclusif et endogène. Au cours de cette session, les délégations ministérielles sont appelées à examiner les activités réalisées au titre de la feuille de route de l’An II, à formuler des recommandations sur la suite du processus et à aborder diverses questions. Les conclusions des échanges devront être consignées dans une note de synthèse destinée à rendre compte des avancées enregistrées dans chaque pilier. Wendyam Pascaline KALMOGO

items.title: Appoint Clowns. Get a Circus
items.description: By Kwame Sowu One of the biggest obstacles to Ghana’s economic and social development is not a shortage of ideas, policies or even resources. It is the chronic appointment of incompetent people to positions that demand competence, leadership and results. Take our Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives. For decades, many have presided over communities that remain filthy, poorly planned, environmentally deplorable and barely liveable. Roads are neglected, drains remain choked, sanitation is appalling, public spaces are abandoned and basic urban management appears to be an alien concept. Yet, somehow, we keep changing governments without changing the conditions in which people live. What exactly do some of these appointees do? Beyond occupying offices, attending meetings, making political appearances and distributing photographs of themselves, what measurable difference have they made to the communities entrusted to them? We must confront an uncomfortable truth: political loyalty is not a qualification for administrative competence. Being a party activist, campaign financier or familiar face in the corridors of political power does not automatically make anyone capable of managing a district, municipality or metropolis. A government can have the most brilliant manifesto, the most ambitious development agenda and the most eloquent presidential speeches. But if the people entrusted with implementation lack imagination, discipline, initiative and basic managerial competence, the outcome is predictable: grand promises, mediocre execution and another four years of excuses. Development is not delivered by manifestos. It is delivered by people who know what they are doing. We must stop treating public appointments as political compensation packages. Critical positions must be occupied by people who can think, organise, innovate, mobilise resources and deliver measurable outcomes. Ghana does not need more ceremonial officeholders. It needs problem-solvers. If we keep appointing people who cannot transform their immediate surroundings, we should stop pretending they will transform a nation.

items.title: Jonas Wétian Koné: une volonté qui voit au-delà des yeux
items.description: Atteint de cécité, Jonas Wétian Koné a connu un début de scolarité tardif. Malgré de nombreuses difficultés, il s'est distingué par ses résultats scolaires. Etudiant en lettres modernes à l'Université Daniel-Ouezzin-Coulibaly de Dédougou, il a terminé major de sa promotion, constituée de plus de 400 étudiants, en 2026. Admis au concours de recrutement des élèves attachés d'intendance scolaire et universitaire, il entame une formation à l'Institut régional d'administration de Fada N'Gourma. Mais il n'entend pas s'arrêter là. Jonas ambitionne de poursuivre ses études supérieures jusqu'au doctorat. Portrait d'un jeune homme dont le parcours est marqué par la persévérance. Un téléphone portable à la main, Jonas Wétian Koné envoie des messages vocaux à des amis. Autour de lui, des enfants du voisinage se sont installés. Les conversations vont bon train. Nous sommes le 25 octobre 2026, au secteur 6 Nord de Fada, où le jeune homme réside avec un frère et une sœur dans le cadre de sa formation à l'Institut régional d'administration (IRA). Elancé, mesurant 1,72 m, il a le teint noir et le visage rayonnant. Sa voix fine traduit une certaine douceur. Attentif à ses interlocuteurs, il se montre disponible dans les échanges. Jonas est l'ami de tous, y compris des plus petits. A 23 ans, il a déjà derrière lui un parcours qui force l'admiration. Pourtant, son histoire n'a pas commencé sous les meilleurs auspices. Né le 6 décembre 2002 à Kéména, un village situé à 17 km de Nouna, dans la province de la Kossi, Jonas est le neuvième enfant d'une famille de 14 enfants. Ses parents sont des cultivateurs aux ressources modestes. A trois ans, une maladie, dont il ignore l'origine et mal soignée, lui fait progressivement perdre la vue, d'abord d'un œil, puis de l'autre. Cette épreuve bouleverse son enfance et compromet son accès à l'éducation. Il a fallu attendre 2012 pour qu'une perspective se dessine. Cette année-là, une structure destinée à accueillir des enfants vivant avec un handicap visuel ouvre ses portes au sein de l'école catholique de Nouna. Un des responsables se rend à Kéména pour informer ses parents de l'ouverture d'une école destinée aux enfants non-voyants. L'annonce ne suscite pas immédiatement l'adhésion de sa mère. Elle craint de se séparer de son jeune fils et doute de ses capacités à suivre une scolarité. Jonas Wétian Koné vise loin dans son parcours. « Elle ne croyait pas que je pourrais avoir une seconde chance dans la vie. Elle ne s'imaginait pas qu'un aveugle pourrait faire l'école », rapporte Jonas. La sensibilisation du responsable finit toutefois par faire évoluer sa position. Elle accepte finalement que son fils parte étudier à Nouna. Une décision qui ouvre une nouvelle page de son existence. Le jeune garçon effectue ses trois premières années à l'école catholique avant de rejoindre l'école primaire du secteur 1 de Nouna. Son père joue un rôle déterminant dans cette étape. Il le transporte à vélo entre le village et Nouna et veille à lui apporter des vivres. Sa sœur, Béatrice Koné, contribue également à son apprentissage. Elle lui fait régulièrement la lecture de documents écrits. A mesure que Jonas avance dans ses études, sa sœur demeure l’une des personnes sur lesquelles, il peut compter pour poursuivre ses apprentissages. Un élève curieux A l'école, le jeune Jonas développe progressivement une véritable passion pour le savoir. Curieux, il cherche constamment à comprendre et n'hésite pas à poser des questions. Il travaille avec ses camarades et leur apporte aussi son aide lorsqu'ils rencontrent des difficultés. Pour lui, la cécité ne doit pas constituer un obstacle aux relations avec les autres. « Je n'ai pas de complexe. Je ne reçois aucun dénigrement de la part de mes camarades de classe. Au contraire, ils me prêtent main-forte. En retour, je les assiste également lorsqu'ils ne comprennent pas une partie du cours », explique-t-il. Cette solidarité marque son ami, Télesphore Taro, son meilleur ami. Les deux se connaissent depuis le lycée provincial de Nouna, mais c'est en classe de terminale que leur proximité se renforce. Ils cheminent ensemble jusqu'à l'université et créent un groupe d’études. Télesphore Taro garde le souvenir d'un camarade disponible. « Quand j'avais des difficultés dans une matière, il me venait toujours en aide parce que lui, il est polyvalent », témoigne-t-il. Jonas se distingue, selon son ami, par son désir permanent de comprendre. « En classe, il ne se contente pas de suivre les cours. Il pose des questions à chaque fois qu'un point lui échappe », précise-t-il. Cette curiosité se prolonge jusque dans les moments de détente. « Au grin, Jonas est à la limite ennuyant. En effet, il ramène toujours les débats sur l’école. Nous ne pouvons même pas discuter d’un autre sujet de la vie pendant longtemps avec lui », plaisante Taro. Au lycée, les déplacements constituent un autre défi. Pour rejoindre son établissement ou rentrer chez lui, Jonas se déplace à vélo, remorqué par un camarade, ou marche avec ses amis. Il lui arrive aussi de parcourir seul le trajet jusqu'à son domicile. Après son baccalauréat, un bienfaiteur lui offre une moto sur laquelle une autre personne le transporte. Un soutien qui facilite ses déplacements et allège certaines contraintes de son quotidien. La récompense au bout de l'effort Depuis le lycée, Jonas s’est fait remarquer par sa rigueur au travail. Derrière cette apparente tranquillité se cachent des moments difficiles. Au lycée, il lui arrive de passer toute une journée sans manger. Parfois, l'envie d'abandonner les études et de retourner à Kéména le tente. Mais les sacrifices de sa famille et sa volonté de réussir le ramènent toujours à la raison. Il mesure les efforts consentis pour lui permettre de poursuivre sa scolarité et ne veut pas renoncer à cette chance. Son oncle Abdoulaye Coulibaly, professeur de lycée, fait partie de ceux qui ont suivi de près cette évolution. Leur rencontre remonte à la classe de sixième. L'enseignant se souvient d'un enfant sage, respectueux et particulièrement intelligent. Formé aux méthodes d'enseignement adaptées, notamment aux signes utilisés en mathématiques, il a pu l'accompagner dans cette discipline. « Ces signes, que tous les enseignants et élèves ne maîtrisent pas, constituent un outil important pour permettre à Jonas de suivre les enseignements », explique-t-il. Le manque de documentation adaptée, confie son professeur, complique l'accès aux connaissances. A cela s'ajoutent les difficultés matérielles et les ressources limitées de la famille. Mais Jonas ne se décourage pas. « Il a vraiment traversé des situations assez difficiles. Mais il a tenu bon », se souvient Abdoulaye Coulibaly. Il l'encourage alors à poursuivre dans cette voie, car, il est sûr que ses aptitudes peuvent le conduire loin. Il souhaite surtout qu'à l'issue de sa formation à Fada N’Gourma, son neveu puisse reprendre ses études et aller au bout de ses ambitions. Les résultats de Jonas témoignent de cette persévérance. En 2018, il obtient le certificat d'études primaires (CEP). Au lycée provincial de Nouna, il décroche le Brevet d’études du premier cycle (BEPC) en 2022 avec 16,50/20, devenant le meilleur élève de sa circonscription. Il bénéficie alors d'un compte d'épargne Coris Bissongo doté d'un million F CFA. En 2025, il confirme ses performances au baccalauréat série A4, obtenu avec 14,96/20. A l'université, les conditions d'apprentissage restent peu adaptées à sa situation. En l'absence d'un système braille, Jonas développe ses propres méthodes de travail. Il enregistre les cours à l'aide d'un dictaphone pour les réécouter. Sa sœur Béatrice Koné et ses camarades l'aident également à accéder aux documents écrits. Les évaluations exigent aussi une organisation particulière. Les sujets lui sont dictés, afin qu'il puisse les saisir sur son appareil. Il travaille ensuite seul, puis dicte ses réponses à une personne chargée de les reporter fidèlement sur sa copie. Après une relecture avec lui, celle-ci est remise avec les autres, sans mention particulière. Les enseignants corrigent ainsi son travail sans savoir qu'il est celui d'un étudiant aveugle. « Jonas ne bénéficie d'aucun traitement de faveur. Il dispose simplement d'un quart de temps supplémentaire, conformément aux textes », rassure le chef de la scolarité de l'Unité de formation et de recherche en Lettres et Sciences humaines, Sié Hien. En lettres modernes à l'Université Daniel-Ouezzin-Coulibaly de Dédougou, à la fin de l'année 2026, il se classe major d'une promotion de plus de 400 étudiants avec une moyenne de 16,02/20. Une satisfaction pour le président de l'université, le Pr Aboudramane Guiro, pour qui ce parcours constitue une source de fierté pour toute la communauté universitaire. « Jonas est la preuve vivante que le handicap n'est jamais un frein à l'excellence lorsque la volonté, le courage et Abdoulaye Coulibaly, professeur des lycées reconnait Jonas Wétian Koné, comme un élève qui visait toujours haut. le travail sont au rendez-vous », affirme-t-il. Son parcours rappelle, selon lui, que l'inclusion dans le système éducatif est une richesse. Admis en 2026 au concours de recrutement des élèves attachés d'intendance scolaire et universitaire de la fonction publique, Jonas poursuit sa formation à l'IRA de Fada N'Gourma. Mais cette étape ne constitue pas un aboutissement. Il envisage de reprendre ses études après sa formation et nourrit l'ambition de décrocher un doctorat. Son rêve professionnel est de transmettre le savoir. « Mon métier de rêve, c'est d'être professeur, parce que j'aimerais transmettre mes connaissances à mes frères et sœurs qui ont un quelconque handicap », confie-t-il. Jonas Wétian Koné souhaite également que les acteurs du système éducatif, des élèves aux enseignants, soient davantage sensibilisés à la situation des personnes vivant avec un handicap. « Sans l'appui d'une personne, c'est difficile », insiste-t-il. Sur le plan sentimental, Jonas file le parfait amour depuis la classe de terminale. « C'est l'amour qui nous unit. La fille est gentille et, depuis qu'on se connaît, je n'ai jamais eu de regrets », confie-t-il. Il envisage de construire un foyer avec sa compagne, mais préfère attendre la fin de sa formation pour officialiser leur union. De Kéména aux bancs de l'université, Jonas Wétian Koné a appris à avancer malgré les obstacles. Pour ce jeune homme qui rêve de devenir docteur, le chemin est loin d'être achevé. Adama SEDGO

items.title: Championnat national de Teqball 2026 : Cléopas Ouédraogo et Wendpanga sur le toit du Faso
items.description: La Fédération burkinabè de Teqball a organisé, le samedi 7 novembre 2026, à l’Université virtuelle du Burkina Faso, les finales du championnat national. Cléopas Ouédraogo en individuel et le club Wendpanga, en double, ont été sacrés. Une édition marquée également par l’engagement des filles et la mise en lumière des jeunes talents. Le Teqball burkinabè poursuit son petit bonhomme de chemin. Après une première édition organisée en 2025, la Fédération burkinabè de Teqball a tenu, le samedi 7 novembre 2026, les finales de son championnat national à l’Université virtuelle du Burkina Faso. Au terme d’une journée de compétition, Cléopas Ouédraogo et le club Wendpanga ont inscrit leurs noms au palmarès de cette deuxième édition. En finale du simple, Cléopas Ouédraogo était opposé à Valentin Karambiri, dans une affiche qui a tenu les spectateurs en haleine jusqu’au bout. Les deux adversaires ont livré une bataille particulièrement serrée. Cléopas Ouédraogo a d’abord pris les devants en remportant la première manche sur le score de 7 à 2. Mais, Valentin Karambiri a réagi dans le deuxième set, qu’il a remporté 7 à 6, relançant ainsi complètement la rencontre. Il a donc fallu un troisième set pour départager les deux finalistes. Dans cette manche décisive, les deux joueurs sont restés au coude-à-coude jusqu’à six points partout. Mais, au moment de conclure, Cléopas Ouédraogo a fait preuve de davantage de maitrise pour s’imposer 9 à 7, pour décrocher ainsi le titre national en simple. Luc Bamouni, champion sortant, complète le podium à la troisième place. En double, la finale a également offert un air de revanche par rapport à l’édition précédente, avec les mêmes protagonistes. La paire de Wendpanga, composée de Cléopas Ouédraogo et Luc Bamouni, retrouvait celle de l’Avenir, constituée de Valentin Karambiri et Gaël Ouattara. Cette fois, le dernier mot est revenu à Wendpanga. Après un premier set remporté sur le score de 7 à 6, Cléopas Ouédraogo et son partenaire ont confirmé leur supériorité dans la deuxième manche (7-3), s’adjugeant le titre national en double. ASK termine à la troisième place. Au-delà des résultats sportifs, cette deuxième édition a été marquée par une participation féminine et une attention particulière accordée à la relève. Des prix spéciaux ont notamment récompensé plusieurs distinctions, dont celle du plus jeune athlète et de la meilleure joueuse. Pour le président de la Fédération burkinabè de Teqball, Rasmané Sawadogo, le bilan est largement positif. « Nous venons de terminer la phase finale du championnat du Teqball 2026 et, comme vous l'avez dit, tout s'est bien passé. Donc, naturellement, nous sommes satisfaits », a-t-il déclaré. Il a particulièrement salué l'engagement des filles, qui ont pris part à la compétition et sont même allées jusqu'en finale. Il a également relevé le doublement des récompenses et la valorisation des meilleurs jeunes, signe de la volonté de la fédération de miser sur la relève. Sur le plan technique, le directeur technique de la Fédération a lui aussi affiché sa satisfaction. Il a souligné une amélioration du niveau des athlètes par rapport à la précédente édition, aussi bien au niveau national que dans les régions. Il a notamment salué les prestations de la région du Nando et de certains clubs, dont les performances ont contribué à rehausser le niveau de la compétition. Cette édition a réuni 21 équipes en simple, réparties en cinq poules, et huit équipes en double, réparties en deux poules. Une participation qui témoigne de l'intérêt grandissant pour cette discipline, dont la fédération ambitionne d'élargir davantage la pratique. « Nous sommes en train, tout doucement, d'étendre notre Teqball sur tout le territoire burkinabè », a indiqué le président Rasmané Sawadogo. Après le Nando, le Nakambé et le Kadiogo, la Fédération entend poursuivre son implantation dans d'autres régions, notamment le Yadéga, le Nazinon, Oubri et le Guiriko. L'objectif est de faire du Teqball une discipline davantage connue et pratiquée à travers le pays, tout en offrant aux jeunes Burkinabè un cadre d'expression et de performance. Pengdwendé Achille OUEDRAOGO

items.title: 2027: APC using my name to gain sympathy – Sule Lamido
items.description: By Muhammad Inuwa, Dutse Former Jigawa State Governor, Sule Lamido, has accused the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of using his name to gain political sympathy in the state ahead of the 2027 general elections. Lamido made the allegation on Tuesday while reacting to Vice-President Kashim Shettima’s declaration at the APC presidential campaign rally in Dutse that all four former governors of Jigawa State, including Lamido, were now supporting the ruling party. Shettima had, during the rally, declared that Jigawa was firmly behind the APC, claiming that all four former governors of the state, including Lamido, a founding member of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), were now associated with the ruling party. However, Lamido dismissed the claim as false and unfounded, alleging that the APC was attempting to associate itself with influential opposition figures to gain public sympathy. He argued that the ruling party could not point to significant achievements in Jigawa State and the wider Northern region, hence its alleged attempt to claim the support of prominent opposition politicians. “I am not aware of what Vice-President Kashim Shettima was saying. For God’s sake, I was not with the APC in 2014, so why would I be with it now in 2026?” Lamido queried. The former governor challenged the APC to identify its achievements in Jigawa and other parts of the North, arguing that its inability to demonstrate meaningful accomplishments had made it resort to associating itself with influential Northern politicians. Lamido, however, outlined conditions under which he would consider joining the APC before the 2027 general elections, challenging President Bola Tinubu’s administration to address insecurity in the North. He specifically mentioned kidnapping, Boko Haram insurgency, banditry and other security challenges, saying their resolution would make him reconsider his political position. “I swear to God, if they end kidnapping, Boko Haram, banditry and all the evils in the North, I will definitely join the APC because whatever we are doing, we are doing it for our people,” he said. The post 2027: APC using my name to gain sympathy – Sule Lamido appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ablekuma West: Roni Nicol declares third bid for NPP parliamentary candidacy
items.description: Roni Nicol, a long-standing member of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), has declared his intention to contest the party’s parliamentary primary in Ablekuma West ahead of the 2028 general elections. The declaration marks his third attempt to become the party’s parliamentary candidate for the constituency, having contested the position in 2016 and 2024. Mr Nicol said his decision was informed by more than 20 years of service to the party, which he described as loyal, selfless and humble. He also highlighted his longstanding connection to the constituency, saying he had lived, schooled and worshipped there for more than 30 years. “For over 30 years, Ablekuma West has been my home. I schooled here, I worship here, I grew here. Ablekuma West is my heart,” he said. Mr Nicol said his previous electoral contests and grassroots political experience had prepared him to lead the NPP in its bid to reclaim the parliamentary seat from the National Democratic Congress (NDC). He pledged to pursue an inclusive campaign focused on job creation for young people, support for businesses and unity within the party. He also called for accountable leadership and urged party members to work together towards victory in the 2028 elections. “Together, let us win back Ablekuma West. Together, let us give our people a united, humble and accountable representation they deserve,” he said. He appealed to delegates and constituents for their support and prayers as the party prepares for the 2028 electoral contest.

items.title: Jimmy Aglah takes the fight against galamsey into Ghanaian classrooms
items.description: Kumasi, Ghana — Ghanaian author and media executive Jimmy Aglah is taking the national conversation on illegal mining, environmental destruction and responsible citizenship into the classroom following the approval of his novel, When the River Testified , by the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NaCCA) as supplementary reading material for Ghanaian students. The NaCCA verification system lists the book as officially approved, identifying it as a supplementary reader for JHS/SHS and confirming that it meets the Council’s standards. At a time when Ghana continues to grapple with the devastating consequences of illegal and irresponsible mining, popularly known as galamsey, When the River Testified seeks to help young people understand not only the environmental damage involved, but also the deeper questions of responsibility, leadership, silence, greed and the choices communities make when confronted with wrongdoing. Set in the fictional Ghanaian town of Asempa Nkwanta, the novel follows broadcast journalist Kofi Densu, whose investigation into a deteriorating river gradually uncovers a much wider environmental and public health crisis. Scientific tests conducted by Dr Mensima reveal elevated levels of mercury and lead in water and food crops. Evidence from the clinic, borehole, palace and surrounding community gradually comes together, forcing residents to confront the consequences of environmental degradation and the failure of individuals and institutions to act. Although fictional, the issues explored in the novel mirror a national challenge that has become increasingly urgent. For Aglah, bringing the subject into literature for young readers is an attempt to move the conversation beyond enforcement and political debate. “We cannot wait until our children become adults before teaching them why the rivers matter, why forests matter and why individual choices have consequences for entire communities,” he said. “The fight for our environment must also be fought in the classroom, in the imagination and in the values we pass on to the next generation.” Aglah believes fiction offers a particularly powerful way of engaging young people because it allows them to encounter environmental issues through characters, consequences and moral choices rather than through statistics alone. The approval of When the River Testified also places the book within Ghana’s broader educational objective of developing learners who can think critically, solve problems, exercise responsible citizenship and apply knowledge to real-life challenges. The book also speaks directly to the international agenda on Education for Sustainable Development. Under Sustainable Development Goal 4.7, the United Nations calls for all learners to acquire the knowledge and skills needed to promote sustainable development, sustainable lifestyles, responsible citizenship and an appreciation of humanity’s relationship with the wider world. The themes of When the River Testified also connect naturally with SDG 6, which seeks access to clean water and sustainable management of water resources, while its treatment of environmental stewardship, degraded land and community responsibility touches on the broader sustainability agenda. Aglah argues that the long-term solution to environmental destruction cannot depend exclusively on arrests, task forces and regulation. “Laws are important, enforcement is important, but sustainability ultimately depends on what a generation believes,” he said. “If young people grow up understanding that poisoning a river is not simply an environmental offence but an attack on health, livelihoods, food security and the future, we begin to build a different kind of citizen.” The author hopes the novel will be used not simply for individual reading, but also as a resource for guided classroom discussion, literature lessons, reading clubs, environmental clubs and values-based education. Teachers, he believes, can use the story to encourage learners to interrogate competing interests, examine evidence, discuss moral responsibility and propose solutions to environmental problems within their own communities. The approval therefore comes at a significant moment in Ghana’s continuing debate over galamsey and the sustainability of the country’s natural resources. Rather than presenting environmental protection as an abstract national policy issue, When the River Testified brings the consequences home through the lives of ordinary people living beside a river whose condition becomes a testimony against human choices. For Aglah, that is ultimately the purpose of the book. “The river in the story cannot walk into a courtroom. It cannot organise a demonstration or hold a press conference. But it can testify through what happens to the people who depend on it. I want young readers to understand that nature eventually presents its evidence.” With NaCCA approval secured, attention now turns to publishing, nationwide distribution and partnerships that can make the book available to schools and young readers across Ghana. Aglah is currently engaging publishers and organisations interested in education, literacy, environmental sustainability and youth development to support the production and wider distribution of the book. When the River Testified is written by Jimmy Aglah and has been officially verified by NaCCA under Book ID NaCCA/G.42/Vol.8/366. For publishing, educational and partnership enquiries: Jimmy Aglah Email: aglahjames@gmail.com

items.title: Niamey : la Route transsaharienne s’affirme comme un futur corridor économique africain…
items.description: Le ministre nigérien de l’Équipement et des Infrastructures, le Colonel-Major Salissou Mahaman Salissou, a reçu le Secrétaire général du Comité de liaison de la Route transsaharienne, accompagné de l’ambassadeur de la République algérienne démocratique et populaire au Niger. Cette audience s’inscrit dans les préparatifs de la prochaine session du Comité de liaison et traduit la volonté des États concernés d’accélérer la transformation de cet axe stratégique en un véritable corridor économique. La rencontre a permis d’échanger sur les perspectives de développement de la Route transsaharienne, un projet majeur reliant l’Algérie au Nigeria sur près de 10 000 kilomètres et traversant notamment le Niger, la Tunisie, le Mali et le Tchad. Le Niger occupe ainsi une position déterminante dans cette infrastructure destinée à renforcer la connectivité entre l’Afrique du Nord et l’Afrique subsaharienne. Au-delà de sa dimension routière, le projet vise désormais à soutenir les échanges commerciaux, encourager les investissements et favoriser l’interconnexion économique entre les pays membres. Lors de la 77e session du Comité de liaison, tenue à Alger, les États membres ont réaffirmé leur ambition de faire de la transsaharienne un corridor économique intégré au service du développement régional. Pour le Niger, cette dynamique ouvre des perspectives importantes en matière de transport, de commerce transfrontalier, de logistique et de valorisation des potentialités économiques le long de l’axe. La coopération avec l’Algérie, illustrée par la présence de l’ambassadeur algérien à Niamey, constitue également un levier pour renforcer les échanges et approfondir le partenariat entre les deux pays. La prochaine session du Comité de liaison devra préciser les priorités et les actions concrètes à mener pour concrétiser cette vision. L’enjeu est de passer d’une infrastructure de liaison à un moteur durable d’intégration économique, capable de bénéficier aux populations, aux opérateurs économiques et aux États traversés par la Route transsaharienne. Par Tamtaminfo News L’article Niamey : la Route transsaharienne s’affirme comme un futur corridor économique africain… est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: En Côte d’Ivoire, la mosquée de Bouna renoue avec sa splendeur
items.description: L’Afrique de l’Ouest compte des dizaines de mosquées de style soudanais : Djenné au Mali, Bobo-Dioulasso au Burkina Faso, Larabanga au Ghana. Identifiables par leur construction en terre et leur architecture particulière, certaines sont classées au patrimoine mondial de l’Unesco, d’autres non. Ces dernières, moins protégées, se dégradent au fil du temps. Un projet tente de les sauvegarder, et pour les plus abîmées, de les restaurer. C’était le cas fin octobre dans le nord de la Côte d’Ivoire, à Bouna, ville à la frontière du Ghana et du Burkina Faso. Pendant deux semaines, des ouvriers venus de divers pays ont travaillé à sauver cette mosquée fragilisée par le temps et le changement climatique, tout en formant d’autres artisans.

items.title: Trump’s Stance on Jensen Huang Is a Tell
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Sometimes a news story is important because it reveals information for the first time. Other times, it’s a big deal because it confirms what many people already suspected. The latest development in the story of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang falls into the second category. As news of Huang’s extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy rocks Silicon Valley, Washington, and Wall Street, President Trump has pleaded ignorance. In particular, he has said he was unaware of the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (no relation) when he traveled to China this past May. “No, I didn’t hear about it then,” he told reporters on Monday. Almost immediately, The New York Times reported that in fact Trump had been warned by Marco Rubio, the national security adviser and secretary of state, while headed to China on Air Force One, just before Jensen Huang boarded the plane for a state visit. (In fact, Trump may have been told even before then: The paper previously reported that Trump was notified about intelligence findings on the relationship last year as well .) The new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, wants to crack down on leaks ; he clearly has his work cut out for him. A few important features of Trump’s approach to the presidency are on display here. First, he has abandoned the pretense of being tough on China, a major talking point during his first presidential run and term. Second, he ignores any intelligence findings that contradict his instincts . Third, this is the latest evidence that, as I wrote last January, Trump does not care about U.S. national security . That doesn’t mean he’s actively hostile to it, or a saboteur; he’s just indifferent to anything but his own interests. In the nearly two years since I first laid out this argument, the president has repeatedly bolstered the case. When Trump was informed that China had infiltrated a tech company that is widely regarded as essential to the health of the global economy as well as a crucial force for maintaining American power and national security—such that the U.S. bans exports of its most powerful chips to China—Trump opted to do nothing and pretend he hadn’t heard. We can only speculate on the reasons. Trump enjoys closeness with titans like Huang and wouldn’t want to endanger that. Huang clearly relished putting Trump on speakerphone during a podcast taping in September. (A serial philanderer himself, Trump said in recent days that Huang “probably has an excuse for” the affair.) The president may have also worried about the risk to the economy of any Nvidia turmoil—both because of the midterm elections and because his own portfolio has grown enormously during the AI boom. Trump was similarly indifferent to the national-security risks of the war in Iran. (Some of his advisers reportedly understood this but did little to dissuade him.) The administration couched the war in terms of eliminating the threat of a nuclear Iran, but given that U.S. intelligence had deemed the program moribund, and given that the Trump administration had claimed to have destroyed the program in 2025, the justification made little sense. And by embarking on a war with no clear strategy or planning, the U.S. has badly depleted its stores of missiles and other munitions, which will spell danger in the event of another conflict. The war has created divisions among American allies and shown that the United States is unable to win a war or guarantee freedom of navigation in the Persian Gulf, all of which weaken its long-term strategic positioning. Not every decision is as consequential as the Iran war, but Trump has repeatedly chosen personal or short-term political gain over American security and national priorities. Accepting the gift of a 747 from Qatar was neither ethical nor a wise security choice—as became clear when Trump had to do his Turkish tarmac turnaround and board a safer plane in August. The president chose his own interests—both flattery and a splashy if minor diesel-fuel deal—in once more embracing Vladimir Putin and distancing himself from Ukraine in October. And as I argued in September , Trump’s decision to treat Venezuela as a vassal state and stifle the popularly supported María Corina Machado is likely to harm American regional interests over time while yielding limited benefits now. To paraphrase Benjamin Franklin , those who would choose some short-term personal benefit over long-term national interest may end up losing both. If Trump hoped that overlooking Huang’s liabilities would prevent turmoil, the bet didn’t pay off. The Wall Street Journal reported this evening that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang, after a report late today of another affair , this one with a subordinate. Huang’s behavior has become both a political scandal and an economic liability, after Nvidia’s stock slid over the past few days. What harm this whole incident may have done to national security may not be clear for months or years to come. Related: A scandal at the center of the economy America can’t afford an AI recession . Here are four new stories from The Atlantic : Jonathan Chait on the left’s election denial The Christian nationalists have a plan. The David Frum Show : Can Republicans quit Trump? The Democrat who wants to make politics boring Today’s News The White House warned incoming House Oversight Committee Chairman Robert Garcia that the Trump administration “will not be extorted” by congressional investigations, cautioning that certain actions could amount to “blatant criminality.” Garcia rejected the warning, saying Congress will not be deterred by “baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President's lawyers.” Russia and Ukraine agreed in principle to a large prisoner exchange after two days of U.S.-mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi ended without a major breakthrough. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff are scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin tomorrow before traveling to Ireland to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. A 41-year-old U.S. Army officer assigned to a NATO unit in Britain was arrested yesterday on suspicion of spying for Russia , British police said. The officer, who had access to sensitive information, remains in custody as British and U.S. authorities investigate, while the Kremlin denies any involvement. Dispatches Work in Progress : Rogé Karma reports on the perverse reason health-care costs are about to surge . Explore all of our newsletters here. Evening Read Mirrorpix / Getty The Stealth Friendship Killer By Olga Khazan Scientists have identified the three leading killers of mom-friend plans: the never-ending day-care virus, the sitter who bailed, and the mysterious vortex that is “out of town.” The first two are unavoidable, but the third is a choice that society, collectively, seems to be making more and more. Out of town is where all of your friends are when you’ve finally decided to host a playdate. Out of town is where everyone is for the entirety of August. Want to grab a drink? I would love to, but I am, well, you get it. Several caveats apply. We don’t know whether Americans are actually making more weekend trips; the most recent large-scale, comprehensive assessment on the topic was conducted in 1995 . The most common reasons that Americans gave last year for not spending more time with their friends were their own mental-health issues, not having enough money, and being too busy ; travel didn’t appear anywhere in the top six. And going away is not an entirely bad thing. Read the full article. More From The Atlantic David Hume Kennerly: “What I saw every step of the way” Modi is facing “a million mutinies.” The worst thing about AI writing The case against a “religious left” Chaim Saiman: Democrats should cut a deal with Trump. Culture Break Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic Read. What Remains , a new book by the Galician writer Brais Lamela, chronicles the drive that many have to touch history, no matter how elusive it is , Lily Meyer writes. Explore. Kelsey Ables traces how ugly metro sweaters became chic . Play our daily crossword. Rafaela Jinich contributed to this newsletter. items.title: Le ministère des Affaires étrangères et la CDC s’allient pour moderniser les cartes consulaires
items.description: Le ministère de l’Intégration africaine, des Affaires étrangères et des Sénégalais de l’Extérieur et la Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations (CDC) ont signé, lundi 9 novembre 2026, une convention spécifique portant sur la modernisation du système de production et de gestion des cartes consulaires. Cette initiative vise à simplifier les démarches administratives des Sénégalais établis à l’étranger et à renforcer la sécurisation de leurs documents. La modernisation des services consulaires franchit une nouvelle étape. Le ministre de l’Intégration africaine, des Affaires étrangères et des Sénégalais de l’Extérieur, Cheikh Niang, et le directeur général par intérim de la Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations (CDC), Amadou Lamine Guissé, ont procédé à la signature d’une convention spécifique destinée à mettre en place un système moderne et sécurisé de production et de gestion des cartes consulaires. À travers ce partenariat, les deux institutions entendent améliorer la qualité des services administratifs proposés aux Sénégalais de l’extérieur. Le dispositif envisagé devrait notamment contribuer à simplifier les procédures d’obtention des cartes consulaires et à garantir une meilleure fiabilité de ces documents. Pour assurer la mise en œuvre opérationnelle du projet, la CDC s’appuiera sur sa filiale SYNAPSYS Conseil SA, spécialisée dans l’accompagnement technologique et le développement numérique. Cette convention s’inscrit dans la dynamique de modernisation de l’administration sénégalaise, avec un accent particulier sur les services destinés à la diaspora. Elle traduit la volonté des autorités de rapprocher davantage les services publics des compatriotes établis hors du territoire national, tout en renforçant la sécurisation des documents consulaires à l’échelle internationale.
